domains.name: Academic Grammar
domains.summary: This domain covers the grammatical resources that carry meaning in academic registers, prioritised by what corpus research shows academic writing actually does rather than by a general-English syllabus order. Its centre of gravity is the noun phrase: academic prose compresses information into premodified and postmodified noun phrases and nominalisations far more than conversation does, so learners need both to unpack such phrases when reading and to build them when writing. Clause-level resources (tense, voice, modality, subordination, complement and reporting clauses) are treated in terms of the rhetorical choices they serve, such as currency in citation, agency in methods and degrees of commitment in claims. Accuracy topics are framed as monitoring and editing problems as much as knowledge problems, and the grammar of spoken academic interaction is treated on its own terms rather than measured against writing.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn the grammar academic texts use most, such as long noun phrases, tense and voice, and how it shapes your claims. You will also learn to find and fix your frequent errors.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Secure clause analysis, agreement, tense, the passive for process description, relative clauses and basic subordination with textbook-level texts, and introduce noun-phrase expansion and the grammar of discussion through description, definition and seminar tasks.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Consolidate tense, voice, articles and noun-phrase postmodification for essays and reports, introduce reporting structures for source-based writing, and build personal error monitoring tied to the progression assignment.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Assume most clause-level grammar and move quickly to phrasal complexity, nominalisation, reporting structures and tense in literature-based writing, with error monitoring geared to the extended project of the target programme.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Address grammar through students' disciplinary reading and assessed drafts, focusing on nominalisation, noun phrases, passive versus active choices and recurrent errors flagged in feedback.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Concentrate on tense in literature reviews, nominalisation, stance-bearing structures and editing efficiency under the time pressure of a short taught programme.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine information packaging (clefts, fronting, end-weight), voice and tense choices in research genres and independent self-editing for publication.

domains.name: Sentence Construction & Punctuation
domains.summary: This domain covers how clauses are combined into well-formed sentences, how punctuation marks grammatical structure and meaning, and how sentence-level choices (length, concision, end-weight) affect readability. Punctuation is treated as a consequence of clause and phrase analysis rather than as a list of rules, and conventions that vary by style guide (serial commas, quotation marks, capitalisation, title case) are taught as choices to be applied consistently. Sentence-level style is grounded in what corpus research shows about academic prose, in particular that its difficulty comes mainly from dense noun phrases rather than from long chains of clauses. The style of numbers and units in running text is covered with the language of quantity in num.number-expressions.
domains.learnerSummary: You will learn to build clear, correctly punctuated sentences and apply the conventions your department or style guide expects. You will also learn to edit sentences so readers can follow dense ideas.

stageEmphasis.foundation: Establish sentence types and boundaries, core comma use, apostrophes, capitals and basic quotation punctuation in short assignments, and introduce list formatting.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-ug: Consolidate boundary and punctuation accuracy under time pressure, including quotation punctuation for source-based essays, and introduce semicolons, colons and control of sentence length.
stageEmphasis.pre-sessional-pg: Assume basic boundary control and focus on concision for word-limited extended projects, semicolons and colons in dense prose, quotation conventions in literature-based writing and early work on end-weight.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-ug: Address the style-guide conventions departments require and sentence-level clarity in assessed reports and essays, with low-level mechanics handled through self-access.
stageEmphasis.in-sessional-pgt: Focus on concision and end-weight in dissertations and data-heavy writing; mechanics are handled through proofreading checklists rather than taught sessions.
stageEmphasis.pgr: Refine sentence-level clarity, end-weight and house-style conventions for theses and journal submission.

topics.name: Clause elements and sentence analysis
topics.description: Identify the subject, verb, object, complement and adverbial of a clause, including when each is realised by a long phrase or an embedded clause, and use this analysis to find the core of dense academic sentences and to build complete ones. Clause analysis supplies the working metalanguage on which later grammar, punctuation, reading and self-editing work depends.
masteryEvidence: Marks the full subject, the finite main verb and any object or complement in academic sentences whose subjects run to ten or more words
Identifies the head noun of a long subject noun phrase and separates it from its modifiers
Distinguishes obligatory complements (depend on X, result in Y) from optional adverbials using a deletion test
Reduces a 40-word textbook sentence to a grammatical core statement and paraphrases what it claims
Uses clause-element labels to explain why a draft sentence is incomplete or ungrammatical
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three authentic 30–45-word sentences from an introductory textbook in the learner's field. Ask the learner to underline the finite main verb, bracket the whole subject and circle its head noun. Check whether they choose the main-clause verb rather than a verb inside a relative or non-finite clause, and whether the subject bracket includes all postmodifiers.

topics.name: Subject–verb agreement with complex subjects
topics.description: Make finite verbs agree with the head of the subject when modifiers separate the two, and handle academic cases where number is not transparent: 'the number of' versus 'a number of', proportion and quantity expressions, coordinated subjects, collective nouns and nouns such as data, criteria and research. Agreement slips are highly visible to markers and editors even when meaning is clear.
masteryEvidence: Produces correct agreement when the head noun and verb are separated by prepositional phrases or relative clauses
Selects singular agreement after 'the number of' and plural after 'a number of' with plural nouns
Applies a consistent, field-appropriate choice for 'data' and correct number for criteria, phenomena and analyses
Finds and corrects agreement errors in a draft by locating each head noun before checking the verb
Explains why some agreement choices (collective nouns, 'data') vary by variety, discipline and house style
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give six sentences with long postmodified subjects, two quantity expressions and one 'data' sentence, with the verb offered as a choice (is/are, has/have). Ask the learner to choose and justify each answer by naming the head noun. Look for justification by head noun rather than nearest noun, and for awareness that 'data' usage varies rather than an absolute rule.

topics.name: Noun-phrase premodification
topics.description: Build and interpret noun phrases with adjectives, participles and nouns before the head (a carefully designed longitudinal study; carbon emission reduction targets), including the order of premodifiers and the implicit meaning relations in noun + noun sequences. Premodification is a major and growing resource for compression in academic writing, and it is a frequent source of both comprehension difficulty and ambiguity.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the head noun in premodified sequences of three or more words and paraphrases the relations between modifiers and head
Chooses the correct word-class form for a premodifier slot (an economic analysis, an economics department, a well-funded project)
Uses nouns as premodifiers where field conventions expect them, without producing ambiguous stacks of four or more nouns
Orders multiple premodifiers acceptably (evaluative before descriptive before classifying)
Rewrites an over-long premodified phrase with a postmodifier when clarity requires it
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five noun phrases from the learner's discipline with two to four premodifiers (for example 'student satisfaction survey data'). Ask the learner to unpack each into a clause or a phrase with 'of/for/about'. Check whether they identify the head and infer plausible relations between nouns; then ask them to compress three short clauses into premodified noun phrases and check word-class choice and order.

topics.name: Noun-phrase postmodification
topics.description: Use and parse the structures that follow a head noun: prepositional phrases (by far the most frequent postmodifier in academic prose), relative clauses, non-finite clauses and appositive noun phrases or clauses. Postmodified noun phrases let writers specify and qualify referents precisely, and they produce the long subjects that many readers, including users of English as an additional language, find demanding to process.
masteryEvidence: Marks the boundaries of postmodifiers in long noun phrases, including stacked prepositional phrases (the effect of X on Y in Z)
Expands a bare noun into a precise noun phrase with a prepositional phrase, a reduced relative and an appositive, as the context requires
Chooses the preposition that a head noun requires (an increase in, the relationship between, a reduction of/in)
Converts a relative clause into a prepositional or non-finite postmodifier, and back, without changing meaning
Identifies attachment ambiguity in stacked postmodifiers and resolves it by reordering or splitting
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 35-word sentence whose subject contains two prepositional phrases and a reduced relative clause. Ask the learner to bracket each postmodifier and say which noun it modifies, then write their own noun phrase describing a variable in their field using at least two postmodifiers. Check attachment, preposition choice after the head, and whether the verb still agrees with the head.

topics.name: Nominalisation and grammatical metaphor
topics.description: Express processes and qualities as nouns (X increased sharply → the sharp increase in X), and logical relations inside the clause as verbs, nouns or prepositions (because X rose, Y fell → the rise in X caused a fall in Y), so that they can be classified, evaluated, made the subject of further clauses and used to carry given information forward, and unpack nominalisations when reading. Writers also need to recognise the costs: nominal style can hide agency and causal relations and can make prose harder to process than necessary.
masteryEvidence: Converts a clause into a nominal group with the correct derived noun, preposition and transformed modifiers (rapidly → rapid)
Unpacks a nominalised sentence into clauses that make agents and causal links explicit
Uses a nominalisation to summarise the previous sentence and make it the theme of the next
Identifies where a nominalisation obscures who did what and restores an agent when the argument needs it
Explains why nominalisation density differs between, for example, a lab report and a reflective account

Rewrites a conjunction-linked pair of clauses as a single clause in which the relation is expressed by a verb, noun or preposition (because → led to, resulted in, the reason for, due to) and explains what becomes less explicit
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a pair of linked sentences in congruent, clause-based form (The government reduced funding. Because of this, universities recruited more international students.). Ask the learner to rewrite them as one sentence using nominalisation, then to unpack a dense nominal sentence from a set text. Check derived-noun accuracy, preposition choice, whether causal meaning survives compression, and whether unpacking recovers the agents.

topics.name: Phrasal versus clausal complexity
topics.description: Understand that academic writing is complex mainly through compressed phrases (noun phrases with premodifiers and prepositional postmodifiers, nominalisations), whereas conversation elaborates through dependent clauses, and use this understanding to read dense prose and to set realistic development goals. The insight corrects the widespread belief that 'academic' means long sentences with many subordinate clauses.
masteryEvidence: Explains, with examples, how a written academic sentence and a spoken explanation of the same content distribute information differently
Identifies the phrasal features (noun premodifiers, prepositional postmodifiers, nominalisations) that make a given sentence dense
Revises a clause-heavy paragraph into a more compressed version and judges whether readability has been lost
Distinguishes complexity that serves precision from complexity that merely lengthens sentences
Recognises that compression makes some meaning relations implicit and checks that the intended relation is recoverable
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a transcript extract of a lecturer explaining a concept and a published paragraph on the same concept. Ask the learner to list three ways the written version packs information differently. Look for observations about noun phrases and nominalisation rather than only 'longer words' or 'more formal vocabulary'.

topics.name: Articles in academic writing
topics.description: Choose between a/an, the and zero article according to countability, specific versus generic reference, first versus subsequent or otherwise identifiable mention, and postmodification (the role of X; zero article with uncountable and plural generic nouns). Article choices encode whether a reader can identify a referent and whether a claim is general or specific, so they matter for meaning as well as accuracy.
masteryEvidence: Uses zero article with uncountable and plural nouns for generic statements (Education improves…; Universities face…)
Uses 'the' for referents identifiable from prior text, shared knowledge or a following of-phrase or relative clause
Distinguishes generic singular ('The mitochondrion is…') from specific reference in definitions and explanations
Explains an article choice in own writing in terms of identifiability and countability rather than memorised lists
Corrects the article errors that most affect meaning before those that are merely conventional (such as with names of theories or institutions)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 120-word paragraph from the learner's field with all articles removed. Ask the learner to restore them and to justify three choices aloud. Check whether justifications appeal to identifiability, genericity and countability, and whether errors cluster on generic reference or on postmodified nouns.

topics.name: Determiners and quantifiers
topics.description: Select determiners and quantifiers that match the countability of the noun and the precision the claim needs: few versus a few, much versus many, less versus fewer, each versus every, a number of, the majority of, a proportion of. Quantifiers carry evaluative and hedging meaning (few studies versus a few studies), so choices affect the claim as well as accuracy.
masteryEvidence: Matches quantifiers to countable and uncountable academic nouns (much research, many studies, little evidence)
Explains the difference in stance between 'few studies have examined' and 'a few studies have examined'
Uses proportion quantifiers (the majority of, a minority of, almost all) in line with the data being described
Applies a consistent policy on less/fewer with count nouns in formal writing while recognising usage variation
Avoids vague quantifiers (a lot of, lots of, plenty of) in formal writing without over-claiming precision
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short table showing how many of 40 studies found a given effect, and ask the learner to write three sentences describing it using different quantifiers. Check countability agreement, the fit between quantifier and numbers, and whether they can explain the gap between 'few' and 'a few'.

topics.name: Tense and aspect in academic writing
topics.description: Use present simple for generalisations, definitions and the content of texts and figures; past simple for completed procedures and specific past studies or events; and present perfect for developments whose relevance continues into the present state of a field. Academic prose relies overwhelmingly on the simple present, with perfect and progressive aspects comparatively rare, so the skill is choosing the marked forms purposefully and keeping tense consistent within a section.
masteryEvidence: Uses present simple for generalisations and for describing what a figure, table or text shows
Uses past simple consistently for completed procedures in methods and for describing a specific study's actions
Uses present perfect to signal that past research or change is still relevant (Several studies have shown…)
Maintains tense consistency within a paragraph and explains any deliberate shift
Avoids progressive forms where a simple form expresses a general or completed state
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short methods paragraph and a short literature-review paragraph with all main verbs in base form. Ask the learner to supply tense and aspect and to justify two contrasting choices. Check whether choices follow function (generalisation, completed procedure, continuing relevance) rather than a single rule such as 'academic writing uses present tense'.

topics.name: Tense when reporting research
topics.description: Choose tense in citing and reporting sentences to signal how the writer positions the cited work: past for a specific study's actions or findings, present perfect for an area of continuing activity, and present for claims the writer treats as currently valid or for what a source argues. Tense correlates with citation form (integral versus non-integral) and reporting-verb choice, and it varies by discipline.
masteryEvidence: Uses past tense to report what a specific researcher did or found and present tense to report claims treated as currently valid
Uses present perfect to summarise a strand of research (Several studies have examined…) before narrowing to specific studies

Explains how, in fields where past tense is the default for reporting studies, a shift to present tense can present a finding as current and generalisable, and why in fields that report positions in the present (Smith argues…) tense alone does not signal endorsement
Keeps tense choices consistent with the citation form chosen and with the conventions of the target discipline
Identifies tense patterns in a literature review from their own field and states the norms they observed
topics.assessmentPrompt: Show the learner three versions of a citing sentence that differ only in tense (Smith found / has found / finds that X). Ask what each version implies about the status of the finding and the writer's view. Look for answers that link tense to currency and generality, recognise that endorsement is signalled mainly by the reporting verb (shows versus claims) and that field conventions differ, and do not tie tense only to when the study was published.

topics.name: Passive voice and agency
topics.description: Form passives across tenses and with modals, and choose between active and passive on functional grounds: keeping given information or the topic in subject position, omitting an agent that is unknown, obvious or irrelevant, and foregrounding processes in methods. The passive is common in academic prose, but it is not inherently 'objective'; writers also need to know when an active verb with a human or 'we' subject is clearer or expected, and how passives interact with dangling modifiers.
masteryEvidence: Forms passives accurately with simple, perfect and modal verb phrases (have been reported, may be attributed to)
Justifies a voice choice in terms of topic continuity, agent relevance or genre convention rather than objectivity
Rewrites a passive sentence as active when the agent matters to the argument (for example when attributing a decision or a claim)
Avoids passives with intransitive verbs (*was happened, *was arisen) and uses passive change-of-state verbs only when an agent is implied (the rate increased / the dose was increased)
Repairs dangling constructions in which an introductory participle clause has no matching subject after a passive main clause
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a methods paragraph written entirely in the passive and a discussion paragraph in which a passive hides who made a claim. Ask the learner to decide which sentences should stay passive and which should change, giving a reason for each. Check whether reasons refer to topic continuity and agent relevance, and whether they mention discipline norms on 'we'.

topics.name: Epistemic modal verbs
topics.description: Use and interpret may, might, could, would, should and must to express degrees of likelihood and inference, including modal + perfect for past inferences (may have contributed) and modal + passive (could be explained by). Modal verbs are a core grammatical resource for hedging and inference, and learners need to separate their epistemic meanings from obligation and ability meanings.
masteryEvidence: Distinguishes epistemic from deontic and ability uses of the same modal in academic sentences (must as inference versus obligation)
Ranks may, might, could, would and must by strength of commitment in context and selects one that matches the evidence
Forms modal perfect and modal passive structures accurately for inferences about past events and causes
Interprets 'would' in academic writing as tentative assertion or hypothetical consequence rather than past habit
Avoids stacking modals with other hedges so heavily that the claim disappears
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give four claims about a set of results that differ only in the modal verb. Ask the learner to rank them by certainty and say which best matches a stated piece of evidence (for example a small correlational study). Check ranking accuracy and whether they reject 'must' and unmodalised assertion as over-claiming for weak evidence.

topics.name: Conditionals and hypothetical reasoning
topics.description: Use real and unreal conditionals and conditional subordinators (if, unless, provided that, assuming that, as long as) to state the conditions under which a claim holds, to reason about hypothetical cases and counterfactuals, and to describe dependencies in methods and models. In academic writing, conditionals do much of the work of limiting and qualifying claims rather than describing imaginary situations.
masteryEvidence: Uses present-tense conditionals to state general dependencies and boundary conditions (If the sample is small, estimates are unstable)
Uses unreal and past unreal conditionals to argue about counterfactuals and alternative explanations
Selects among if, unless, provided that and assuming that according to the logical relation intended
Recognises inverted conditionals (Were X to…, Had the study…) in formal texts and uses them sparingly where they suit the register
Interprets conditional claims in sources correctly, including what they do not assert
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short claim (Raising the minimum wage reduces employment) and ask the learner to rewrite it as three qualified claims using different conditional forms or subordinators. Check whether the conditions are logically appropriate, tense and modal choices are accurate, and 'unless' is used with the correct polarity.

topics.name: Defining and non-defining relative clauses
topics.description: Form and punctuate defining and non-defining relative clauses with which, that, who, whom, whose and preposition + which/whom (the extent to which, the conditions under which), and recognise reduced relatives. The defining/non-defining distinction changes what a sentence claims about a set of referents, so commas here carry meaning, not just style.
masteryEvidence: Explains the difference in meaning between a defining and a non-defining version of the same sentence
Punctuates non-defining clauses with commas and avoids commas around defining clauses
Uses preposition + which/whom where the verb or noun requires it (the extent to which, the theory on which)
Uses whose for possession with non-human antecedents where appropriate in formal writing
Avoids resumptive pronouns inside relative clauses (*the method which we used it)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give two sentences that differ only in commas (The participants who completed the survey were paid / The participants, who completed the survey, were paid). Ask the learner who was paid in each case. Then ask them to combine three pairs of sentences using a relative clause, one requiring preposition + which. Check the meaning explanation, punctuation and pronoun choice.

topics.name: Non-finite clauses
topics.description: Use -ing, -ed and to-infinitive clauses as postmodifiers (the factors affecting uptake; the data collected in 2020), adverbials of purpose, means and result (To test this, …; thereby reducing …) and complements, so that information can be added without a full finite clause. Because non-finite clauses have no expressed subject, writers must ensure the implied subject is recoverable and avoid dangling participles.
masteryEvidence: Reduces relative clauses to -ing or -ed postmodifiers, choosing the participle that matches active or passive meaning
Uses to-infinitive clauses of purpose in methods writing and -ing clauses of result (thereby, thus causing) in explanations
Ensures that the implied subject of an introductory participle or infinitive clause is the subject of the main clause
Identifies and repairs dangling participles in own and peers' writing
Interprets the logical relation (time, cause, means, result) implied by a non-finite adverbial clause in reading
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give four sentences: two with full relative clauses to reduce, one with a dangling participle and one with an ambiguous -ing clause. Ask the learner to reduce, repair and explain. Check participle choice (affecting versus affected), whether the repair aligns subjects, and whether the learner can name the implied logical relation.

topics.name: Subordination and adverbial clauses
topics.description: Combine clauses with subordinators that express reason, concession, contrast, condition, purpose and time (because, since, although, whereas, while, so that, once), placing the subordinate clause before or after the main clause according to information flow. Subordinators make logical relations explicit within the sentence and are central to concession and explanation, even though academic prose relies less on finite adverbial clauses than conversation does.
masteryEvidence: Selects a subordinator that expresses the intended relation (although for concession, whereas for contrast, since for reason)
Avoids double marking of the same relation (*Although X, but Y; *Because X, so Y)
Places a subordinate clause initially when it sets up given information or a concession, and finally when it carries new information
Writes concessive sentences that acknowledge a counter-position before asserting the writer's own
Distinguishes subordinators from linking adverbials and punctuates each correctly (although versus however)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give pairs of related clauses and ask the learner to combine each with a different subordinator expressing a specified relation (concession, contrast, reason, purpose). Check choice of subordinator, absence of double marking, clause order and punctuation of initial subordinate clauses.

topics.name: Coordination and parallel structure
topics.description: Coordinate words, phrases and clauses with and, but, or, nor and correlative pairs (both … and, either … or, not only … but also) so that coordinated elements share the same grammatical form, especially in lists, comparisons and aims or research questions. Faulty parallelism makes relations between ideas harder to follow, and phrasal coordination is itself a resource for compression in academic writing.
masteryEvidence: Produces lists whose items share one grammatical form (to identify…, to compare… and to evaluate…)
Places correlative conjunctions immediately before the parallel elements (not only in X but also in Y)
Identifies and repairs faulty parallelism in own aims, research questions and bullet lists
Uses phrasal coordination to combine related information without repeating whole clauses
Avoids ambiguity in coordinated modifiers (older men and women) by repeating or reordering elements
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a set of three study aims written in mixed forms (to identify X, comparing Y, and an evaluation of Z) and a sentence with a misplaced 'not only'. Ask the learner to revise both. Check that all aims share a form and that correlatives sit before matching constituents.

topics.name: That-clauses and wh-clauses
topics.description: Use that-clauses and wh-/whether-clauses as noun clauses after verbs (suggest that, examine whether), adjectives (clear that, unclear how) and nouns (the claim that, the question of whether), and as subjects. Complement clauses are the main grammatical frame for reporting and evaluating propositions, and the noun + that-clause pattern is a characteristic way of labelling claims in academic prose.
masteryEvidence: Uses that-clauses after reporting and stance verbs, retaining 'that' in formal writing
Forms embedded questions with statement word order (examine how X affects Y, not *how does X affect Y)
Uses whether-clauses for yes/no embedded questions in aims and research questions
Distinguishes appositive noun + that-clauses (the claim that X is false) from relative clauses (the claim that X made)
Selects adjectives and nouns that license complement clauses (It is likely that; the assumption that)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to turn three direct research questions into embedded clauses in a statement of aims (This study examines…), and to complete two sentences beginning 'The finding that…' and 'The finding that the team…'. Check word order in embedded questions, choice of whether/if, and whether the learner can explain the difference between the two 'finding that' sentences.

topics.name: Anticipatory 'it' and extraposition
topics.description: Use anticipatory it with an extraposed that-, to- or wh-clause (it is important to note that; it has been argued that; it remains unclear whether) to place a heavy clause at the end of the sentence and to express stance without self-mention. These frames are frequent in academic writing, but they can also add empty words and obscure who holds a view.
masteryEvidence: Forms extraposed structures with adjective, verb and passive frames followed by that-, to- or whether-clauses
Chooses an anticipatory-it frame whose evaluative meaning matches the intended stance (possible, likely, clear, surprising)
Rewrites an anticipatory-it sentence with an explicit agent when attribution matters (It is argued that → Smith argues that)
Removes anticipatory-it frames that add words without adding stance (It is important to note that…) where appropriate
Distinguishes anticipatory it from referring it in reading and writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with five anticipatory-it frames, two of them attributionally vague (It is believed that…). Ask the learner to classify each by the stance it expresses and revise the vague ones. Check whether they identify evaluative meaning and restore attribution where needed, rather than simply deleting all frames.

topics.name: Existential 'there' constructions
topics.description: Use existential there + be to introduce new entities, evidence or developments (there is evidence that; there has been a shift towards; there are three reasons for), with agreement controlled by the following noun phrase. The structure presents new information at the end of the clause, and a frequent learner error is to follow it directly with a finite verb (*There are many people think…).
masteryEvidence: Uses existential there with present, past and present perfect forms of be in academic contexts
Makes be agree with the notional subject (there is little evidence; there are several limitations)
Repairs *There are many people think… using a relative clause or by deleting 'there are'
Uses existential frames to introduce evidence or gaps (there is little research on…) rather than as a default opening
Varies openings so that existential there does not dominate a paragraph
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three erroneous sentences (*There are many studies show…; *There have a debate…; *There is many factors…). Ask the learner to correct each in two ways if possible. Check whether they choose between a relative clause and deleting 'there are', and handle agreement and the be/have confusion.

topics.name: Comparative structures
topics.description: Compare quantities, qualities and cases precisely with comparative and superlative forms, degree modifiers (considerably, slightly, markedly higher than), multiplicative comparisons (twice as likely as; three times the rate of), proportional comparisons (the more…, the more…) and prepositional frames (compared with/to, in comparison with, relative to). Comparison is central to data commentary, compare–contrast writing and evaluation, and imprecise or illogical comparison is a common source of unclear claims.
masteryEvidence: Forms comparatives and superlatives accurately, including with long adjectives and irregular forms
Uses degree modifiers that match the size of a difference in data
Expresses multiplicative and proportional relations accurately (twice as high as; three times higher than is avoided where ambiguous)
Compares like with like using that of / those of (the rate in X is higher than that in Y)
Uses the more… the more… structure and prepositional comparison frames accurately
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a small table with values for three groups and ask the learner to write four comparative sentences, including one multiplicative comparison and one using 'that of' or 'those of'. Check logical comparison of like with like, accuracy of multiplicatives, and whether degree modifiers match the data.

topics.name: Prepositions and complex prepositions
topics.description: Use dependent prepositions after verbs, nouns and adjectives (focus on, impact on, consistent with) and complex prepositions (in terms of, with respect to, in contrast to, due to, owing to, as a result of) accurately, recognising both their grammatical attachment and their meaning. Prepositions are high-frequency, largely lexically governed and hard to infer, so learners need to treat many of them as parts of larger units.
masteryEvidence: Uses the dependent preposition required by frequent academic verbs, nouns and adjectives
Selects complex prepositions by meaning (in terms of for dimension, with respect to for scope, in contrast to for contrast)
Uses 'due to' and 'owing to' in ways accepted by the target style, aware that some editors still prefer 'due to' after be
Checks uncertain preposition choices against a learner dictionary or corpus
Avoids overusing 'in terms of' as an all-purpose link
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give eight sentences with prepositions removed after common academic verbs, nouns and adjectives, plus two sentences where a complex preposition must be chosen. Check accuracy and ask the learner how they would check uncertain items.

topics.name: Cleft and pseudo-cleft sentences
topics.description: Use it-clefts (It is X that…) and wh- or pseudo-clefts (What this suggests is…) to place one element in focus, typically for contrast or correction, and recognise what clefts presuppose. Clefts are a marked information-structure resource: used sparingly they direct the reader to the key point; overused they sound emphatic or speech-like.
masteryEvidence: Forms it-clefts and wh-clefts accurately with nominal, adverbial and clausal focus
Uses an it-cleft to contrast or correct a previous or expected claim (It is not X but Y that…)
Uses a wh-cleft to foreground a conclusion or the writer's main point at a paragraph turn
Distinguishes it-clefts from anticipatory-it extraposition in reading and writing
Limits clefts so that each one marks a genuine point of contrast or focus
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short paragraph that sets up a common assumption and ask the learner to write a sentence correcting it with an it-cleft and a concluding sentence with a wh-cleft. Then give two sentences beginning 'It is…' and ask which is a cleft. Check accuracy, contrastive purpose, and the cleft/extraposition distinction.

topics.name: Fronting and inversion
topics.description: Recognise and use marked word orders in formal writing: fronted complements with subject–verb inversion (Of particular concern is…; Central to this argument is…), inversion after fronted negative or restrictive elements (Not only does X…, Only when… does…, Rarely have…), and fronted adverbials. These structures link to preceding text or create emphasis, but they are infrequent and easily overused, so the target is controlled, occasional use and accurate comprehension.
masteryEvidence: Forms inversion with the correct operator after fronted negative and restrictive elements (Not only does…, Only then can…)
Uses a fronted complement with inversion to link a new, heavy subject to the preceding discourse
Explains the information-flow reason for a fronted structure found in a published text
Rewrites an over-marked sentence in canonical order when fronting adds no linking or contrast
Parses sentences with fronted elements correctly when reading
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three canonical sentences that follow a context sentence and ask the learner to rewrite one with a fronted complement and inversion and one with 'Not only…'. Then ask them to explain why the third should stay in canonical order. Check operator choice and whether the fronted element links to the context.

topics.name: Placement and punctuation of linking adverbials
topics.description: Place linking adverbials (however, therefore, thus, moreover, consequently, nevertheless) in initial, medial or final position and punctuate them correctly, recognising that they link sentences rather than join clauses. Medial placement is comparatively common in academic prose and can put focus on the element before the adverbial; the main accuracy problem is the comma splice created by using however or therefore as if it were a conjunction.
masteryEvidence: Punctuates linking adverbials between independent clauses with a full stop or semicolon, never a comma alone
Places however and therefore medially after the subject or first auxiliary when the subject is the contrastive or given element
Varies position so that sentence-initial connectors do not dominate a paragraph
Distinguishes linking adverbials from conjunctions and subordinators with similar meanings (however/but/although; therefore/so)
Uses thus and hence correctly with clauses and, in the case of thus, with -ing clauses of result
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with five linking adverbials, all sentence-initial, including two comma splices. Ask the learner to repair the splices and move two adverbials to medial position. Check the repairs and whether medial positions are grammatical and placed after the element being contrasted.

topics.name: Reporting structures
topics.description: Control the grammatical patterns used to report sources: reporting verb + that-clause (argues that), + noun phrase (questions this assumption), + noun + as (describes X as Y), + wh-clause (examines how), passive and raising patterns (X is thought to…; It has been suggested that…), and adjunct frames (according to X; as X argues; in X's view). Accurate patterns let writers attribute content precisely and signal the extent of attributed material.
masteryEvidence: Uses the complementation pattern each frequent reporting verb requires (discuss X, not *discuss about X; describe X as Y)
Uses adjunct frames (according to, as X notes) without mixing them with a reporting verb (*According to Smith, he argues that…)
Uses passive and raising patterns (X is considered to be…) while making clear who holds the view when it matters
Varies reporting structures across a paragraph to avoid repeating one frame
Places citation references correctly in integral and non-integral reporting sentences
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give five erroneous reporting sentences (for example *Smith discussed about…; *According to Lee, she claims that…; *Jones described the policy is a failure). Ask the learner to correct them and to write two new reporting sentences about a source they know, using different patterns. Check verb complementation and the separation of adjunct and verb frames.

topics.name: Pronoun and demonstrative reference
topics.description: Use it, they, this, these, that, those and the former/the latter so that each has a clear antecedent, and choose 'this + noun' (this approach, these findings) when a pronoun alone could refer to several things or to a whole preceding clause. Clear reference is a basic condition of cohesion, and ambiguous 'this' or 'it' is one of the most frequent clarity problems tutors identify.
masteryEvidence: Identifies the antecedent of every pronoun and demonstrative in own paragraph, and revises where two candidates exist
Adds a summarising noun after this/these when reference is to a clause or stretch of text
Matches number between demonstrative and antecedent (these data, this criterion, these criteria)
Uses the former and the latter only when exactly two antecedents are close by
Explains how style guides and expert practice differ on the use of 'this' without a noun
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with three ambiguous pronouns or demonstratives. Ask the learner to identify every possible antecedent and revise. Check whether they detect ambiguity, add an accurate summarising noun, and avoid replacing every pronoun with a noun repetition.

topics.name: Ellipsis and substitution
topics.description: Avoid unnecessary repetition with substitute forms (do so, one/ones, that of, those of, the same) and with ellipsis in coordinated and comparative structures, while ensuring the omitted or substituted element is recoverable. These resources contribute to cohesion and concision, and 'that of/those of' is essential for logically valid comparisons.
masteryEvidence: Uses that of and those of with correct number agreement in comparisons
Uses do so to substitute a verb phrase where repeating it would be clumsy
Uses one and ones to substitute countable nouns, not uncountable ones
Uses ellipsis in coordinated clauses without leaving the omitted element ambiguous
Judges when repetition of a key term is clearer than substitution
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a paragraph with repetitive structures and an illogical comparison (The salary of nurses is lower than doctors). Ask the learner to revise using substitution and ellipsis. Check that the comparison becomes logical, number agreement is correct, and key terms are not replaced where precision requires repetition.

topics.name: Monitoring recurrent grammatical errors
topics.description: Identify one's own persistent error patterns from feedback and self-analysis, prioritise those that most affect meaning and reader judgement, and build targeted editing routines (error logs, single-focus editing passes, checklists) that reduce them over time. Because many errors persist as performance slips rather than gaps in knowledge, self-monitoring is the main route to accuracy beyond the EAP classroom.
masteryEvidence: Keeps an error log that records error type, an example from own writing and a correction
Identifies three to five personal priority error types from feedback across several assignments
Edits a draft in separate passes for each priority error type rather than reading once for everything
Distinguishes rule-governed errors that can be self-corrected from lexical choices that need a resource or an informant
Shows a reduction in the frequency of logged error types across successive pieces of writing
topics.assessmentPrompt: Ask the learner to bring two marked pieces of writing and identify their three most frequent error types, with examples. Then ask them to edit a new paragraph for those types only. Check whether priorities are grounded in evidence, whether the editing pass catches errors, and whether the learner can explain the rule or strategy for each.

topics.name: Grammar of spoken academic interaction
topics.description: Recognise and use the grammar typical of spoken academic interaction (heads and tails, situational ellipsis, clause chaining with and, so and because, discourse markers such as so, right and I mean, and vague category markers such as and so on or that kind of thing), and decide which accuracy features matter most for being understood in seminars, tutorials, group work and presentations. Speech follows different grammatical norms from writing, so learners need neither to speak in written sentences nor to treat normal spoken features as errors.
masteryEvidence: Identifies heads, tails, situational ellipsis and clause chaining in a transcript of a seminar or tutorial exchange and explains what each does for the listener
Uses short elliptical responses (Probably not; Same here; Depends on the sample) in discussion instead of repeating full clauses
Uses a fronted head or a clarifying tail to introduce or pin down a topic when explaining an idea to peers (This model, it assumes…; It's quite dated, that study)
Uses discourse markers and vague category markers to manage talk, and replaces them with specific content when the listener needs precision

Keeps the features most likely to affect understanding in speech accurate (verb forms that carry time or certainty, negation, clear reference) while using spoken features that would be edited out of writing
Adjusts grammatical choices between an informal group discussion and a formal presentation segment
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a two-minute transcript of students discussing a reading that includes a head (This model, it assumes…), elliptical replies and a long and-so chain. Ask the learner which features would be changed in a written summary and which work well in speech, then ask them to answer a seminar question orally for one minute. Check whether they treat spoken features as legitimate rather than as errors and whether their own answer keeps tense, negation and reference clear.

topics.name: Genitive and noun-modifier choices
topics.description: Choose between the s-genitive (the study's aims; Piaget's theory; the region's population), the of-phrase (the aims of the study) and a noun premodifier (study aims) according to the animacy, length and information status of the modifying noun and to field convention, and avoid long chains of of-phrases. Inanimate s-genitives are well established in published academic prose, so the school rule that 's is only for people is a simplification, not a norm.
masteryEvidence: Rewrites a phrase in all three forms (the model's accuracy / the accuracy of the model / model accuracy) and explains which suits a given sentence
Uses an of-phrase when the modifying noun phrase is long or carries new information (the accuracy of the model proposed by Lee) and a genitive or premodifier when it is short and given
Uses s-genitives with inanimate possessors (the study's limitations, the region's population) where they read naturally, without avoiding them on principle
Revises chains of three or more of-phrases into clearer noun phrases using a genitive, a premodifier or a clause
Forms genitives accurately, including plural possessors, and does not combine an article with a proper-noun genitive (*the Smith's theory)
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give six noun phrases, including an of-chain (the results of the analysis of the data of the survey), two inanimate genitives (the study's aims; the country's economy) and a phrase with a long possessor. Ask the learner to give the alternative forms for each and to choose the best one for a given sentence, explaining why. Check whether choices reflect possessor length, given–new order and clarity rather than a blanket rule against inanimate 's, and whether genitive forms are accurate.

topics.name: Unaccusative and ergative verbs
topics.description: Use intransitive verbs that describe events without an agent (occur, happen, arise, emerge, appear, exist) in the active voice, avoiding overpassivised forms such as *was happened and *was emerged, and choose between intransitive and passive uses of ergative change-of-state verbs (the temperature increased / the temperature was increased; prices rose / prices were raised) according to whether an agent is implied. These choices are frequent in process description, methods and data commentary, where voice shows whether a change is presented as spontaneous or caused.
masteryEvidence: Uses occur, happen, arise, emerge, appear and exist only in the active voice in own writing
Chooses between intransitive and passive uses of change-of-state verbs (prices rose / prices were raised; the rate increased / the dose was increased) according to whether an agent is implied
Uses transitive–intransitive pairs such as rise/raise and fall/lower or reduce with the correct transitivity and verb forms
Explains how a voice choice in a methods or results sentence changes whether a change appears spontaneous or caused
Finds and repairs overpassivised intransitive verbs in a draft
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a short process or results paragraph with gaps for six verbs (occur, emerge, increase, decrease, raise, change), with context that makes clear whether an agent caused each change. Ask the learner to fill each gap with an active intransitive or a passive form and to justify two choices. Check for *was occurred-type forms and whether the voice of each change-of-state verb matches the presence or absence of an agent.

topics.name: Simple, compound and complex sentences
topics.description: Recognise and build simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences by identifying independent and dependent clauses and the devices that join them (coordinators, subordinators, relative pronouns, punctuation). The classification is a working tool for punctuation and clause combining; it does not measure sophistication, since a long simple sentence with dense noun phrases is typical of academic prose.
masteryEvidence: Identifies independent and dependent clauses in sentences of up to three clauses

Classifies sentences as simple, compound, complex or compound-complex and justifies the classification by counting finite clauses (the pedagogical convention, while recognising that descriptive grammars also count non-finite clauses as dependent clauses)
Combines short sentences into compound and complex sentences using a joining device that expresses the intended relation
Explains why a dependent clause cannot stand alone as a sentence in formal writing
Recognises a long single-clause sentence with heavy noun phrases as grammatically simple but informationally dense
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give six sentences from a textbook, including a 35-word sentence with one finite verb and heavy noun phrases built only from adjectives, nouns and prepositional phrases (no non-finite or relative clauses). Ask the learner to mark clause boundaries and classify each sentence. Check that they count finite clauses rather than words and do not label the long single-clause sentence as complex.

topics.name: Sentence boundaries
topics.description: Mark sentence boundaries so that every written sentence contains an independent clause and independent clauses are joined only by a coordinator, a semicolon or a colon, avoiding comma splices, fused (run-on) sentences and unintended fragments. Boundary errors are highly visible to markers and can obscure the logical relation between ideas.
masteryEvidence: Identifies and repairs comma splices using a full stop, semicolon, coordinator or subordination
Identifies fragments formed by detached subordinate clauses, participle phrases and 'such as' lists, and attaches or completes them
Repairs fused sentences in which two independent clauses run together without punctuation
Chooses the repair that best expresses the logical relation between the clauses rather than always using a full stop
Distinguishes boundary errors from style choices such as sentence-initial 'And' or 'But', which expert writers sometimes use
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 120-word paragraph containing two comma splices, a detached because-clause and a fused sentence. Ask the learner to find and repair each, using at least three different strategies. Check detection rate and whether each repair expresses the intended relation.

topics.name: Commas in academic prose
topics.description: Use commas after introductory adverbials and subordinate clauses, around non-defining relative clauses, appositives and interrupting elements, and between list items (with a consistent decision on the serial comma), and avoid commas between subject and verb, between a verb and its object or that-clause, and around defining clauses. In academic prose most comma decisions follow from clause and phrase structure, and some (non-defining clauses, serial commas) change or clarify meaning.
masteryEvidence: Places commas after introductory subordinate clauses and long introductory phrases
Encloses non-defining relative clauses and appositives in commas and leaves defining clauses unpunctuated
Avoids a comma between a long subject and its verb and before a that-clause object
Applies the serial comma consistently in line with the target style guide
Explains how adding or removing a comma changes the meaning of a given sentence
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 100-word paragraph with all commas removed, containing an introductory clause, a non-defining relative clause, a list and a long subject. Ask the learner to restore commas and justify three of them. Check for structural justifications and for the absence of a comma between subject and verb.

topics.name: Semicolons and colons
topics.description: Use semicolons to join closely related independent clauses of comparable weight (including before a linking adverbial) and to separate list items that contain internal commas; use colons after a grammatically complete clause to introduce an explanation, elaboration, example, list or quotation. Both marks signal logical relations inside the sentence and are valuable in dense prose, but overuse makes text harder to process.
masteryEvidence: Joins independent clauses with a semicolon only when both are complete and closely related
Uses semicolons to separate complex list items that contain commas
Uses a colon only after a complete clause, not between a verb or preposition and its object
Distinguishes the semicolon's balancing function from the colon's expanding function in own writing
Applies the target style guide's rule on capitalisation after a colon
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give six sentences: two joined by commas that need semicolons, one with a colon after 'such as', one complex list, and two correct. Ask the learner to correct and justify. Check for the complete-clause test before colons and accurate list punctuation.

topics.name: Punctuation and mechanics beyond the comma
topics.description: Apply the conventions for marks and mechanics that markers and editors check routinely: apostrophes for possession but not plurals (the authors' view; 1990s; PhDs), hyphens in compound modifiers before a noun (an evidence-based approach) and en dashes for ranges (pp. 12–18); quotation marks, ellipsis, square brackets and the position of citations and full stops in quotations; and capitals for proper nouns and named theories but not general concepts, with title or sentence case as the target style requires. Some of these choices carry meaning (a small-business owner; an ellipsis that drops a negation from a quotation), while others are style conventions to be applied consistently.
masteryEvidence: Places possessive apostrophes correctly for singular and plural owners and omits them from plurals of acronyms, numbers and decades
Hyphenates compound modifiers before a noun but not after it or after -ly adverbs, and uses an en dash for ranges and relational compounds (a cost–benefit analysis)
Uses ellipsis and square brackets to fit a quotation into own sentence without changing the source's meaning
Places quotation marks, citations and final punctuation in run-in and block quotations as the target style requires, applying one quotation-mark convention consistently

Capitalises proper nouns and named models while keeping general concepts and disciplines in lower case, and applies sentence or title case to headings and reference-list titles as the target style requires
Checks a draft in a final mechanics pass and leaves no inconsistencies in these conventions
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 60-word source passage and a short draft extract with a heading and two reference entries. Ask the learner to quote part of the passage in their own sentence, omitting a phrase and changing one word to fit their grammar, with a citation in the specified style; then ask them to correct ten mechanics decisions in the extract (apostrophes, compound modifiers, a page range, capitalised general concepts, title case). Check fidelity of the quotation, ellipsis and bracket use, citation and full-stop placement, and whether corrections follow the named style consistently.

topics.name: Sentence length and variety
topics.description: Control sentence length for readability and emphasis: split or restructure sentences that overload the reader, combine strings of short sentences whose logical relations need to be explicit, and use a short sentence to state a key claim or turning point. Sentence length is a weak index of academic quality, so the aim is length chosen for purpose rather than long sentences as a marker of sophistication.
masteryEvidence: Identifies sentences in own writing that contain more than one main claim plus several embedded clauses and restructures them
Combines short consecutive sentences when the relation between them (cause, contrast, concession) needs to be stated
Uses a short sentence to foreground a key claim after longer explanatory sentences
Varies sentence openings and structures so that consecutive sentences do not repeat one pattern
Explains why sentence length alone does not make writing more academic
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 150-word paragraph that contains one 70-word sentence and a run of five very short sentences. Ask the learner to revise it for readability and explain two decisions. Check whether the long sentence is split at logical points, the short sentences are combined with explicit relations, and the key claim is made prominent.

topics.name: Concision
topics.description: Remove redundancy, empty phrases and wordiness (due to the fact that → because; in order to → to; each and every → each), replace light verb + nominalisation with a verb where no compression benefit results (carry out an analysis of → analyse), and cut unnecessary repetition, without stripping the hedges, qualifications and signposting the reader needs. Concision serves word limits and readability, but it is not the same as brevity.
masteryEvidence: Replaces wordy multi-word expressions with shorter equivalents where meaning is unchanged
Replaces empty light-verb constructions with single verbs while keeping nominalisations that do summarising or linking work
Removes redundant pairs and tautologies (past history, final outcome, basic fundamentals)
Cuts a 300-word passage by 15–20 per cent without losing content, hedging or necessary signposting
Distinguishes purposeful hedges and metadiscourse from padding
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a 200-word paragraph padded with wordy phrases, two redundant pairs and one necessary hedge. Ask the learner to cut it by about 20 per cent. Check that padding goes, the hedge and key signposts stay, and no new errors or meaning changes are introduced.

topics.name: Clarity and end-weight
topics.description: Structure sentences so that subject and main verb come early and close together, long or new elements come late (the principle of end-weight), and long pre-verbal subjects or noun stacks do not delay the verb or create ambiguity; use extraposition, the passive, postmodification or splitting to achieve this. These choices reduce the processing load of dense academic prose and align sentence structure with given–new information flow.
masteryEvidence: Revises sentences with long pre-verbal subjects by moving heavy material after the verb or into a separate clause
Places the main verb early in most sentences of own drafts and keeps intervening material between subject and verb short
Uses anticipatory it or a passive to move a heavy clause to the end where this improves flow
Identifies ambiguous noun stacks and rewrites them with postmodification
Explains a revision in terms of reader processing and given–new order rather than personal preference
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give three sentences from a draft: one with a 30-word subject, one with a five-noun stack and one with a that-clause subject. Ask the learner to revise each for clarity and explain the change. Check that the verb moves earlier, heavy material moves later, and meaning is preserved.

topics.name: Lists and bullet points
topics.description: Decide when vertical lists are appropriate (common in reports, proposals, methods, slides and posters; usually discouraged in essays where connected prose is expected) and format both run-in and vertical lists with a grammatical lead-in, parallel items, and consistent punctuation and capitalisation according to the target style. Converting a list into connected prose that makes the relations between items explicit, and vice versa, is a key skill for moving between genres.
masteryEvidence: Judges whether a list is acceptable in a given assignment genre and checks the brief or departmental guidance when unsure
Introduces a vertical list with a lead-in that either is a complete sentence or continues grammatically into each item
Makes all list items parallel in grammatical form
Punctuates and capitalises list items consistently depending on whether they are full sentences or fragments
Converts a bullet list into a cohesive paragraph that states the relations between items
topics.assessmentPrompt: Give a bullet list from a student report with a fragmentary lead-in, non-parallel items and inconsistent punctuation. Ask the learner to fix it, and then to rewrite it as a paragraph for an essay. Check parallelism, lead-in grammar, consistency, and whether the paragraph adds explicit links rather than just removing bullets.

dependencies.reason: Most agreement errors with complex subjects arise from postmodifiers placed between the head noun and the verb; learners must be able to bracket postmodifiers to find the head that controls agreement
Agreement with research, evidence, data, criteria and phenomena depends on knowing each noun's countability and plural form
Premodifier slots require the right word-class variant (economic/economics, well-funded/funding), which depends on control of derivational families
Relative clauses are the most familiar postmodifier and the base from which reduced relatives and other non-finite postmodifiers are taught
Prepositional phrases are the dominant postmodifier in academic prose, and head nouns select particular prepositions (increase in, effect on)
Nominalising a process requires producing the derived noun (analyse → analysis, fail → failure) and transforming adverbs into adjectives
The participants of a nominalised process are expressed as postmodifying prepositional phrases (the increase in X, the analysis of Y by Z)
Noun and adjective premodifiers are one of the two main phrasal resources whose role the concept explains
Nominalisation is the mechanism that turns clausal meanings into phrasal ones; the contrast between clausal and phrasal complexity cannot be grasped without it
The concept is a register contrast (mode: speech versus writing), so an understanding of situational variation frames it
Choice between a/an, the and zero article depends first on whether the noun is countable and singular or plural
Many academic uses of 'the' are licensed by a following of-phrase or relative clause that makes the referent identifiable
much/many, less/fewer and little/few are selected by the countability of the noun
Reporting conventions apply the general meanings of past, present and present perfect to citation; those meanings must already be controlled
Tense choices correlate with integral versus non-integral citation, so learners need that distinction to see the pattern
Passivisation promotes the object to subject and makes the agent optional; learners must identify objects and subjects to form and evaluate passives
Passive verb phrases combine be in the required tense and aspect with the past participle (has been shown, was measured)
Inferences about past events use modal + perfect (may have contributed), which builds on control of perfect aspect
The main clauses of hypothetical and counterfactual conditionals use would, could and might with epistemic meaning
Conditional clauses are adverbial clauses; learners need the main/subordinate clause relation and subordinator placement
Relativisation replaces a subject, object or prepositional object inside the relative clause; choosing who/whom/which and avoiding resumptive pronouns requires that analysis
Non-finite postmodifiers are taught as reductions of relative clauses (the data which were collected → the data collected)
Choosing between -ing and -ed participle clauses depends on recognising active versus passive meaning
Non-finite adverbial clauses express the same relations as finite adverbial clauses without a subordinator or subject, and the implied-subject rule builds on main/subordinate clause analysis
Subordination produces complex sentences; learners need the distinction between independent and dependent clauses first
Time and condition clauses impose tense constraints (no will after once or when for future reference) that build on control of tense
Coordination is introduced as the clause-combining operation that creates compound sentences before it is extended to phrases and lists
Noun clauses are dependent clauses functioning as clause elements inside complex sentences
Learners must distinguish complementiser 'that' after nouns (the claim that X) from relative 'that' (the claim that X made), which presupposes familiarity with relative clauses
Extraposition moves a that- or wh-clause subject to the end of the sentence; the clause types must already be controlled
Many anticipatory-it frames extrapose a to-infinitive clause (it is necessary to…), so infinitive clauses are usually taught first
Repairing the frequent error *There are many people think… requires inserting a relative pronoun
Academic existential frames frequently use present perfect (there has been a shift; there have been few studies), which builds on control of aspect
Comparisons of quantity (more, fewer, less, as many as) depend on quantifier choice by countability
Logical comparison requires the compared elements to be parallel in form and meaning (the rate in X versus that in Y)
Dependent prepositions are best learned as habitual co-occurrences with particular verbs, nouns and adjectives rather than inferred from meaning
It-clefts resemble extraposed structures and are easiest to teach by contrast with anticipatory it, which learners meet first
Clefts exist to assign focus and mark contrast against given information; without the concept of information structure they are used as decoration
Fronting is motivated by linking given material to the preceding text and placing heavy new material late
Inversion after negative or restrictive fronted elements requires selecting the correct operator (does, has, can) from the verb phrase
Placement and punctuation decisions apply to connectors whose meanings and functions learners already know
Joining two independent clauses with however or therefore requires a semicolon or full stop, so learners need control of sentence-joining punctuation
The most frequent reporting patterns are reporting verb + that-clause or wh-clause
Each reporting verb has its own complementation pattern (describe X as Y; question X), which is a case of word grammar
this/these/that/those function both as determiners and as pronouns; the 'this + noun' strategy builds on their determiner use and number agreement
Demonstratives and 'which' often refer to whole clauses; recognising clause boundaries helps writers see what a pronoun could point back to
Substitution and ellipsis are cohesive ties that, like reference, depend on a recoverable antecedent
That of and those of are used mainly in comparisons, so comparative structures are taught first
Error logs are built from coded or direct corrective feedback, so learners need to understand and use correction codes
Targeted error monitoring is a sentence-level editing activity, distinct from global revision; learners need that distinction to schedule it
Spoken grammar is taught as a set of norms appropriate to a mode and situation rather than as error, which presupposes the idea that grammatical choices vary with register
Recognising what situational ellipsis leaves out (a subject, an auxiliary, a verb phrase) and what a head or tail duplicates draws on identifying clause elements
One of the three options is a noun premodifier (study aims); choosing it requires control of noun + noun premodification and head-final order
The of-phrase option is a prepositional postmodifier, and repairing of-chains requires bracketing stacked postmodifiers
Forming singular and plural s-genitives (the author's / the authors') depends on accurate apostrophe placement
Choosing between an intransitive and a passive use of a change-of-state verb, and recognising *was happened as an overpassivisation, presupposes forming passives and knowing that they imply an agent
Whether a verb is intransitive, transitive or both is a lexical property learned with each verb's complementation pattern
Classifying sentences depends on identifying clauses, which in turn requires finding each finite verb and its subject
Comma splices, fused sentences and fragments are defined by the independent/dependent clause distinction
The first constraint on comma use is that a comma alone cannot join independent clauses
Commas around non-defining relative clauses, and their absence around defining ones, follow from the meaning distinction taught with relative clauses
The comma after an introductory subordinate clause presupposes recognising subordinate clauses and their position
Semicolon uses are defined against the comma: joining independent clauses where a comma would splice, and separating list items that already contain commas
Hyphenation of compound modifiers depends on recognising that the compound premodifies a head noun (a long-term study versus in the long term)
Parenthetical dashes are taught as an alternative to paired commas, so comma conventions are usually secured first
The position of the parenthetical citation relative to closing quotation marks and the full stop depends on knowing the in-text citation format
Splitting long sentences and combining short ones safely requires secure control of where sentences can begin and end
Non-finite clauses are a main resource for combining short sentences without adding finite clauses
Phrasal coordination lets writers merge related short sentences while keeping structure transparent
Reducing full relative and adverbial clauses to non-finite clauses is a principal concision technique
Learners need to understand nominalisation to tell purposeful nominal compression from empty light-verb constructions
End-weight problems in academic prose arise mainly from heavy noun phrases; managing them presupposes understanding how phrasal compression creates density
End-weight decisions are justified by the given-before-new principle, which tells writers what to place early and late
Extraposition with anticipatory it is a standard technique for moving a heavy clausal subject to the end
Rewriting of-chains and ambiguous noun stacks for readability draws on choosing among a genitive, an of-phrase and a noun premodifier
Well-formed lists require all items to share one grammatical form
Lead-ins to lists use colons after complete clauses, and complex run-in lists use semicolons
Whether lists are acceptable depends on genre conventions, so learners need the idea that genres carry distinct expectations

guidance.summary: Teach clause elements functionally and with authentic academic sentences: the difficulty in academic text is not finding the subject of a five-word sentence but finding it when it carries several postmodifiers. Keep metalanguage minimal and use it at once for reading (locating the main clause) and for writing (checking completeness). Norris and Ortega's (2000) meta-analysis found explicit instruction effective, although many outcome measures favoured explicit knowledge, and rapid syntactic parsing is one of the lower-level processes L2 academic readers need to automatise (Grabe, 2009).

activities.title: Core-sentence extraction
learnerActions: Take a 35–45-word sentence from a set text and bracket every phrase or clause that could be removed without making the sentence ungrammatical
Remove bracketed material step by step until only subject head, finite verb and any obligatory object or complement remain
Check that the core still makes a grammatical statement and paraphrase it in under ten words
Compare cores with a partner and resolve disagreements with question and pronoun-substitution tests (What was affected? Replace the subject with 'it' or 'they')
activities.intendedInsight: Long academic sentences have a short grammatical core; much of their length is modification of noun phrases.
activities.rationale: Shrinking sentences makes hierarchical structure visible and transfers directly to reading dense prose; corpus evidence that academic noun phrases carry heavy modification explains why subjects are long (Biber et al., 1999).

activities.title: Colour-coding one's own paragraph
learnerActions: Highlight the subject of every main clause in a paragraph of own writing in one colour and the finite main verb in another
Flag any sentence with no finite main verb, or with two main clauses joined only by a comma
Repair flagged sentences and note which problem occurred most often
activities.intendedInsight: The same analysis used for reading also diagnoses fragments and run-on sentences in one's own writing.
activities.rationale: Applying analysis to learners' own output gives the metalanguage a purpose and directs attention to form in meaningful text, consistent with the role of noticing in acquisition (Schmidt, 1990).

difficulties.pattern: The subject is the noun just before the verb.
difficulties.revealedBy: Marking 'participants' as the subject in a sentence such as 'The attitudes of participants towards the intervention were…', and parallel agreement errors in writing.
difficulties.response: Use pronoun substitution (replace the whole subject with 'it' or 'they') and question tests to show where the subject begins and ends. Avoid 'look left of the verb' shortcuts, which fail precisely on academic sentences.

difficulties.pattern: Prepositional phrases are always extras that can be deleted.
difficulties.revealedBy: Deleting 'on X' after 'depends' or 'in Y' after 'resulted' when reducing sentences, leaving ungrammatical cores.
difficulties.response: Contrast verbs that require a prepositional complement (depend on, consist of, result in) with optional adverbials using deletion tests, and connect this to word-grammar patterns.

difficulties.pattern: I know the grammar terms, but I cannot find the main verb in a long sentence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Accurate word-class labelling on short sentences combined with failure to identify subject and main verb in authentic 40-word sentences.
difficulties.response: Build on existing metalanguage but separate word class (form) from clause function, and practise on long authentic sentences rather than relabelling short invented ones.

diagnostic.task: Give a 35-word sentence whose subject contains a prepositional phrase and a relative clause. Ask the learner to say in their own words what the sentence claims, then to mark the full subject and the main verb.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Brackets the full subject including all postmodifiers, identifies the finite main-clause verb and paraphrases the core claim accurately.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Finds the main verb but truncates the subject at the first noun, or paraphrases correctly while marking a relative-clause verb as the main verb.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Labels words only by word class, chooses the first verb in the sentence as the main verb, or cannot state what the sentence claims.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, clause analysis is taught explicitly with textbook sentences and linked to sentence boundaries and agreement. On pre-sessional courses it works best embedded in reading of set texts and editing of drafts rather than as a stand-alone grammar unit. In undergraduate in-sessional provision it is revisited briefly as a tool for parsing disciplinary reading and diagnosing fragments.

guidance.summary: Agreement errors in academic writing are often processing rather than knowledge failures: as subjects lengthen, writers agree with the nearest (attractor) noun. Teaching therefore combines head-noun identification with a targeted editing routine, and treats genuinely variable cases (data, collective nouns, notional concord with quantity expressions) descriptively, as the Longman grammar does (Biber et al., 1999). Ferris (1999) classes agreement among rule-governed 'treatable' errors, which makes it a good candidate for focused feedback and self-editing.

activities.title: Head-noun hunt and attractor test
learnerActions: Bracket the subject in each of ten sentences from a set text and underline its head noun
Draw an arrow from the head noun to the verb and check agreement
In pairs, rewrite two correct sentences by inserting a plural noun into the postmodifier, and challenge a partner to choose the verb
activities.intendedInsight: The verb agrees with the head noun, however far away it is, not with the nearest noun.
activities.rationale: Making the head–verb dependency visible targets the attraction mechanism; agreement is a treatable error type suited to focused attention (Ferris, 1999).

activities.title: Usage check on variable agreement
learnerActions: Search a disciplinary corpus or a set of recent articles from their field for 'data is/are/was/were' and 'a number of … is/are'
Tally the patterns and compare with a partner from a different field
Decide on a policy for their own writing and record it in a personal style sheet
