activities.intendedInsight: Some agreement 'rules' are usage choices that vary by field and house style; consistency matters more than any single prescription.
activities.rationale: Corpus consultation grounds usage judgements in attested examples, and a meta-analysis reports generally positive learning effects of data-driven learning (Boulton & Cobb, 2017), and corpus grammar documents notional as well as grammatical concord (Biber et al., 1999).

difficulties.pattern: I make the verb agree with the noun next to it.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors such as 'The effects of the new policy on students is…' in drafts, which the learner corrects immediately when the sentence is pointed out.
difficulties.response: Treat as a monitoring problem: teach a specific editing pass (find each long subject, locate the head, check the verb). Do not re-teach basic third-person -s as though knowledge were missing.

difficulties.pattern: I forget the -s, even in short sentences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Omitted or inconsistent third-person -s across short and long subjects, typically among writers whose first language has no subject–verb agreement morphology.
difficulties.response: Point out that English marks agreement only in the present tense and on be, a small and checkable set, and give a narrow editing checklist. Combine with focused written corrective feedback on this one category.

difficulties.pattern: Research and evidence are plural because they refer to many studies.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'Researches show…', 'evidences are…', or plural verbs after singular mass nouns.
difficulties.response: Revisit countability, and offer countable alternatives (studies, findings, pieces of evidence) when the writer needs a plural idea.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a three-sentence summary of a small table, using 'the proportion of', 'a number of' and one subject with an of-phrase containing a plural noun.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All verbs agree with the head; 'the proportion of' takes a singular verb and 'a number of + plural' a plural verb; the learner can name the head noun when asked.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Agreement with simple subjects is correct but one attraction error or one quantity-expression error appears, and the learner corrects it when prompted to find the head.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Several agreement errors in simple and complex subjects, and the learner cannot identify the head noun even when prompted.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need both the morphology and the head-finding habit. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work should focus on long subjects in the learner's own drafts. At PGT level the emphasis shifts to quick self-editing passes and to informed choices about 'data' and collective nouns that match the target field.

guidance.summary: Corpus research shows that premodification, especially nouns modifying nouns, is a defining and historically growing feature of academic writing, and that these compressed phrases leave the meaning relation between modifier and head implicit (Biber & Gray, 2010, 2016). Teach learners to unpack premodified phrases as well as to build them, and treat noun premodifiers as an advanced feature: developmental work suggests attributive adjectives appear earlier than noun premodifiers in EAP writing (Parkinson & Musgrave, 2014; Biber et al., 2011).

activities.title: Unpacking noun stacks
learnerActions: Collect five noun phrases with two or more premodifiers from a set text in their field
Paraphrase each with a postmodifier or a clause (student satisfaction data → data about how satisfied students are)
Compare paraphrases and note where the relation between nouns was ambiguous or needed subject knowledge
activities.intendedInsight: Noun + noun sequences compress meaning by leaving relations unstated, and readers recover them with subject knowledge.
activities.rationale: Biber and Gray (2010) argue that academic writing is less explicit than commonly assumed because phrasal modifiers leave relations implicit; making those relations explicit supports both reading and controlled production.

activities.title: Building and ordering premodifiers
learnerActions: Start from a bare head noun relevant to their discipline (study, model, policy)
Add premodifiers one at a time from a given set (evaluative, size or time, classifying, noun), deciding the order
Test the final phrase on a partner: can they paraphrase it? If not, move one modifier after the head
activities.intendedInsight: Premodifier order follows a classifying-closest-to-the-head tendency, and there is a point at which compression stops helping the reader.
activities.rationale: Guided construction targets the feature that distinguishes more advanced EAP writing (Parkinson & Musgrave, 2014), while the readability check guards against over-compression.

difficulties.pattern: If I put the adjective form, it is always correct before a noun.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'An economic department', 'a statistic analysis', or adjectives used where the field uses a noun premodifier (health policy, not 'healthy policy').
difficulties.response: Contrast classifying noun premodifiers with descriptive adjectives using field examples, and use a corpus or term bank to check established combinations.

difficulties.pattern: Writers whose first language places modifiers after the noun build phrases in that order or express everything with of-phrases.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings such as 'the policy of the government of reduction of emissions' or reversed noun + noun order (the reduction emissions).
difficulties.response: Show that English noun + noun compounds put the head last, practise converting of-phrase chains into premodified phrases where the field does so, and accept of-phrases where they are clearer.

difficulties.pattern: Longer noun stacks sound more academic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Stacks of four or five nouns that readers cannot parse (university student mental health support service evaluation).
difficulties.response: Introduce the reader-paraphrase test and model splitting a stack with one postmodifier. Do not ban noun premodifiers, which are central to many fields.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to unpack two premodified noun phrases from a set text and to compress the clause 'a survey that measured how satisfied students were with online teaching' into a shorter noun phrase.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Paraphrases identify the head and plausible relations; the compressed phrase uses correct word classes and order (an online teaching satisfaction survey, or a student satisfaction survey on online teaching) and remains readable.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Unpacks the phrases correctly but compresses with a word-class error, or produces an over-long stack without noticing the loss of clarity.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Misidentifies the head noun or cannot produce any premodified version.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and early pre-sessional learners mainly need adjective and participle premodifiers and the skill of reading noun stacks in textbooks. Later pre-sessional and in-sessional work adds noun premodifiers and disciplinary term formation. At PGT level the focus is on matching field conventions and avoiding ambiguity in dense methods and results writing.
reviewNotes: Premodifier order is presented as a tendency; descriptive grammars disagree on the precise categories, so the order should not be taught as an absolute rule.

Parkinson and Musgrave (2014) are cited only for the broad finding that noun premodifiers were a feature of their more advanced EAP group, consistent with the developmental sequence proposed by Biber et al. (2011); the guidance does not depend on the details of their group comparison. Genitive choice (the study's aims / the aims of the study / study aims) is treated in grm.genitive-noun-modifiers.

guidance.summary: In academic prose, prepositional phrases are by far the most frequent noun postmodifiers, ahead of relative clauses (Biber et al., 1999), and Biber et al. (2011) place prepositional postmodification late in their proposed developmental sequence for writing. Teach postmodification as a resource for precision (specifying which X, under what conditions) and as the main source of long subjects that readers must parse. Practise expansion and reduction in both directions so learners can choose between a relative clause, a non-finite clause and a prepositional phrase.

activities.title: Specify the referent
learnerActions: Start with a vague noun phrase in their own draft (the problem, the results)
Add postmodifiers to specify it: one prepositional phrase, then a reduced relative, then an appositive if needed
Read the sentence aloud and decide which version gives the reader enough precision without overload
activities.intendedInsight: Postmodifiers make reference precise, and different postmodifier types carry different amounts of information.
activities.rationale: Developing the phrasal resources that Biber et al. (2011) associate with advanced academic writing, in the learner's own text, links grammar to precision of meaning.

activities.title: Relative-clause reduction ladder
learnerActions: Take sentences containing full relative clauses (the data which were collected in 2020)
Reduce each to a non-finite clause and then, where possible, to a prepositional phrase or a premodifier (the data collected in 2020; the data from 2020; the 2020 data)
Mark which reductions change or lose meaning, and explain why
activities.intendedInsight: The same meaning can be packaged at different levels of compression, and not all reductions are equivalent.
activities.rationale: Moving between clausal and phrasal options mirrors the clausal-to-phrasal shift documented in academic writing (Biber & Gray, 2010) and gives learners controlled choice rather than one template.

difficulties.pattern: I am not sure which noun this 'of' or 'in' phrase belongs to.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misreading stacked postmodifiers (the effect of temperature on growth in seedlings) or producing ambiguous ones in writing.
difficulties.response: Teach attachment by bracketing and by moving the phrase to test meaning, and show how to resolve ambiguity by reordering or splitting the noun phrase.

difficulties.pattern: The increase of… / the relationship of A and B.
difficulties.revealedBy: Default use of 'of' after head nouns that select other prepositions (in, on, between), often where the first language uses a single all-purpose linking particle or preposition.
difficulties.response: Teach head noun + preposition as a lexical unit and build a personal list of high-frequency academic head nouns with their prepositions, checked against a corpus or learner dictionary.

diagnostic.task: Give a sentence with a subject containing two stacked prepositional phrases and a reduced relative. Ask the learner to bracket each postmodifier, say which noun it modifies, and then write a noun phrase about a variable in their field using at least two postmodifiers.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct attachment for all postmodifiers, correct prepositions after head nouns, and an original noun phrase that is precise and grammatical.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Bracketing correct but own phrase uses a wrong preposition, or own phrase correct but attachment of one stacked phrase misread.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot separate postmodifiers from the main verb or treats each prepositional phrase as a separate clause.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners concentrate on relative clauses and simple prepositional postmodifiers in definitions and descriptions. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners need reduction and attachment for reading and writing source-based texts. At PGT level the priority is precise and unambiguous postmodification in methods, results and literature-review writing.

guidance.summary: Systemic functional work on 'grammatical metaphor' covers ideational metaphor (processes and qualities realised as nouns; logical relations such as cause realised inside the clause as verbs, nouns or prepositions: leads to, the cause of, due to) and interpersonal metaphor (I think → it is likely that). For nominalisation, it explains how processes become things that can be quantified, evaluated and used as given information in the next clause, and why this makes scientific and academic text dense for novice readers (Halliday & Martin, 1993; Schleppegrell, 2004). Teach both packing and unpacking: learners must decode nominal style when reading and use it selectively in writing, noticing when it hides agency or causality. Present nominalisation as a resource with costs, not as a marker of good style.

activities.title: Congruent and metaphorical versions
learnerActions: Take a two-sentence explanation written in everyday clausal form
Rewrite it with nominalisations so that the second sentence begins with a noun phrase summarising the first
Compare the two versions and note what was gained (flow, abstraction) and lost (agents, explicit causality)
activities.intendedInsight: Nominalisation lets a writer pack a process into a noun and carry it forward, at the cost of explicitness.
activities.rationale: Moving between congruent and metaphorical wordings is central to Halliday's account of how written language differs from speech (Halliday, 1989; Halliday & Martin, 1993).

activities.title: Who did what? Unpacking for reading
learnerActions: Choose a dense sentence from a set reading
List each nominalisation and turn it back into a clause with a subject and verb
Decide whether the original text tells the reader who the agents are, and discuss why it might not
activities.intendedInsight: Nominal style can leave agents and causes unstated, which matters for critical reading.
activities.rationale: Making grammatical metaphor visible supports comprehension of school and academic texts (Schleppegrell, 2004) and links grammar to critical reading of agency.

difficulties.pattern: The more nouns I use, the more academic my writing is.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of empty nominalisations with light verbs (carry out an investigation of the analysis of…) that add length but no precision.
difficulties.response: Contrast purposeful nominalisation (to summarise, classify or evaluate) with wordy light-verb constructions, and revise with the concision checklist. Do not swing to banning nominalisation.

difficulties.pattern: The increase of the prices rapidly…
difficulties.revealedBy: Mixed clausal and nominal grammar after nominalising: adverbs left unchanged, wrong prepositions, or missing articles on the new noun phrase.
difficulties.response: Teach the transformations as a set: verb to noun, adverb to adjective, subject to of- or by-phrase, and add a determiner.

difficulties.pattern: I can read each word, but I cannot see what is happening in the sentence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reading comprehension breaks down on sentences with several nominalisations even when vocabulary is known.
difficulties.response: Use unpacking to clauses as a reading strategy and model it on set texts, linking to parsing practice.

diagnostic.task: Give two linked sentences in clausal form and ask the learner to combine them into one using nominalisation; then give a dense nominalised sentence and ask them to unpack it into clauses.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate derived nouns, adjectives and prepositions; causal meaning preserved in the combined sentence; unpacking recovers plausible agents and processes.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Produces nominalisations with one grammatical slip, or unpacks accurately but cannot pack, or vice versa.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot produce the derived nouns or the unpacked version changes the meaning.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional UG courses introduce nominalisation mainly for reading and for summarising. Pre-sessional PG courses teach it productively for literature-based writing and creating flow, because master's writing depends on it. In undergraduate in-sessional work it is linked to disciplinary reading and lab or report writing. PGT and PGR writers need to calibrate nominal density to genre and audience, including lay summaries where unpacking is the goal.

guidance.summary: Biber and Gray (2010) challenge the stereotype that academic writing is complex through elaborated clauses, showing that its distinctive complexity is phrasal and compressed. Biber, Gray and Poonpon (2011) argue that clause-based measures such as subordination are better suited to conversation than to academic writing development, and Lu (2011) found phrase-level measures such as complex nominals per clause discriminated proficiency better than dependent-clause ratios. Teach this as a conceptual reorientation: learners stop chasing long, clause-heavy sentences and start building precise noun phrases.

activities.title: Speech versus writing comparison
learnerActions: Read a short lecture transcript and a textbook paragraph on the same topic
Count dependent clauses and count noun phrases with two or more modifiers in a 60-word stretch of each
Explain to a partner where each text 'puts' its information
activities.intendedInsight: Speech elaborates with clauses; academic writing compresses into noun phrases.
activities.rationale: Direct comparison of registers enacts the corpus finding that clausal and phrasal complexity are distributed differently across speech and academic writing (Biber & Gray, 2010; Biber, 2006).

activities.title: Compress and check
learnerActions: Take a clause-heavy paragraph from their own writing
Rewrite two sentences using noun phrases and nominalisations
Ask a peer to paraphrase the rewritten sentences and judge whether compression helped or hindered
activities.intendedInsight: Compression is a tool to use selectively, judged by whether the reader can recover meaning.
activities.rationale: Applying the concept to one's own writing makes it a development goal rather than an abstract fact, while peer paraphrase tests the readability cost that Biber and Gray (2010) associate with reduced explicitness.

difficulties.pattern: Academic sentences must be long and have many 'which' and 'although' clauses.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of subordinate clauses in essays, often encouraged by test preparation that equated complexity with clause combining.
difficulties.response: Show corpus contrasts and expert paragraphs; redirect effort to noun-phrase precision. Do not discourage subordination outright, which remains necessary for argument.

difficulties.pattern: Now I compress everything, but my tutor says it is hard to follow.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-dense sentences with multiple nominalisations and noun stacks that peers cannot paraphrase.
difficulties.response: Introduce readability checks and the idea that density should match genre and audience; link to end-weight and concision.

diagnostic.task: Give a spoken explanation and a written paragraph on the same topic and ask the learner to describe in two or three sentences how the written version differs grammatically.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies noun-phrase expansion, nominalisation and fewer clauses in writing, with examples from the texts.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Notices that writing is 'denser' or 'uses more nouns' but cannot point to specific structures.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Attributes differences only to vocabulary formality or sentence length.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses the concept reorients learners away from clause-combining habits formed in test preparation. Undergraduate in-sessional work connects it to disciplinary reading load. At PGT and PGR level it supports deliberate control of density, including writing for non-specialist audiences.
reviewNotes: Review response (R6-11): the IELTS Grammatical Range and Accuracy link was removed, because this conceptual topic is not primarily used for test preparation. Audience is set to "both" because the concept also shapes how teachers judge complexity in learner writing (Biber et al., 2011).

guidance.summary: Article choice is semantic (identifiable or not, specific or generic) and depends on countability, which is why learners whose first languages lack articles may find the system persistently difficult even at advanced levels. Master (1997) recommends a simplified, meaning-based system, broadly identification (the) versus classification (a/an or zero), rather than long lists of rules. Prioritise errors that change meaning or affect generic statements and definitions, and teach the of-phrase and relative-clause contexts where postmodification makes the referent identifiable and so licenses 'the', contrasting them with postmodified nouns that still take 'a' or zero (a study of, an increase of 5%, evidence of).

activities.title: Identify or classify?
learnerActions: For each noun phrase in a short academic paragraph, decide whether the writer is identifying a particular referent or classifying it as a member of a type
Predict the article from that decision and countability, then check against the original
Note any cases the decision did not predict and discuss them as conventional uses
activities.intendedInsight: Most article choices follow from whether the reader can identify the referent and from countability.
activities.rationale: Master (1997) argues that a binary, meaning-based approach is more teachable than rule lists and suits the article system's semantic basis.

activities.title: Generic statements in definitions
learnerActions: Write three definitions from their discipline in three forms: plural zero article, singular 'a', and generic 'the'
Compare which forms sound natural for which nouns, using examples from a textbook
Revise own definitions so article use is consistent within a paragraph
activities.intendedInsight: Generic reference has several forms with slightly different uses, and academic definitions favour particular ones.
activities.rationale: Generic reference is a high-frequency academic use that learners often handle by memorised rule; contrasting forms in definitions makes the semantic choice explicit (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

difficulties.pattern: My first language has no articles, so I add 'the' when it sounds right.
difficulties.revealedBy: Omitted articles with singular countable nouns, and fluctuating use of 'the' that tracks specificity rather than definiteness (for example 'the' for a particular referent the reader cannot yet identify; Ionin et al., 2004), in writers whose first languages do not grammaticalise definiteness through articles.
difficulties.response: Teach a small decision sequence (countable? singular? identifiable?) and give focused feedback on one or two high-impact categories at a time. Avoid comprehensive correction of every article, which overloads attention.

difficulties.pattern: My first language has articles, but they work differently.
difficulties.revealedBy: Use of 'the' with generic plurals or abstract nouns (The society, The globalisation) in writers whose first languages use definite articles for generic reference.
difficulties.response: Contrast English zero article for generic plurals and uncountables with the learner's L1 pattern, and practise generic statements specifically.

difficulties.pattern: I know the rules, but I still make mistakes when I write fast.
difficulties.revealedBy: Correct choices in gap-fill tasks but frequent errors in timed writing.
difficulties.response: Build article checking into a separate editing pass rather than expecting accuracy while composing; prioritise noun phrases in key claims and definitions.

diagnostic.task: Remove all articles from a 100-word paragraph in the learner's field and ask the learner to restore them, then explain three choices.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Restores articles with few errors and explains choices by identifiability, genericity and countability, including 'the' where an of-phrase makes the referent uniquely identifiable (the role of X), and 'a' or zero where the postmodifier only classifies (a member of the committee, evidence of bias).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Handles specific reference well but errs on generic statements or uncountables, or relies on memorised phrases for explanations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Errors throughout, with no consistent principle in explanations.

guidance.contextNotes: Article accuracy is a long-term development area, so stages differ in emphasis rather than content. Pre-sessional teaching (UG and PG) establishes the decision sequence and assesses it in writing; foundation courses introduce it alongside countability. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional work concentrates on high-impact errors in assessed writing. For PGR writers, articles are mainly an editing and publication-readiness issue, often handled through targeted self-editing and literacy brokers.
reviewNotes: Generalisations about which L1 backgrounds find articles difficult should be read as tendencies linked to whether the L1 marks definiteness grammatically, not as predictions for individuals.

guidance.summary: Determiners and quantifiers sit at the junction of grammar and stance: 'few studies have examined X' establishes a gap, while 'a few studies have examined X' introduces supporting work. Teach them with countable and uncountable academic nouns and with data, so that the quantifier can be matched to actual proportions. Treat contested usage (less versus fewer with count nouns) descriptively, noting that the distinction is generally maintained in formal written registers (Biber et al., 1999), and replace informal quantifiers (a lot of, lots of) rather than banning approximation.

activities.title: Matching quantifiers to data
learnerActions: Look at a table showing how many of 40 studies report a given effect
Write sentences using few, a few, several, many, most and the majority of
Swap with a partner and check whether each quantifier fits the numbers, and discuss borderline cases (is 12 of 40 'several' or 'a minority'?)
activities.intendedInsight: Quantifiers make approximate claims that must be calibrated to evidence, and some boundaries are matters of judgement.
activities.rationale: Linking quantifier choice to data connects a grammatical system to claim calibration; corpus description shows the range of quantifying expressions in written registers (Biber et al., 1999).

activities.title: Few versus a few in literature reviews
learnerActions: Compare pairs of sentences from literature reviews such as 'Few studies have…' and 'A few studies have…'
Decide which version establishes a research gap and which lists examples
Write two sentences about their own topic using each form deliberately
activities.intendedInsight: A small grammatical difference signals whether the writer is stressing scarcity or presence.
activities.rationale: The contrast is a compact example of grammar carrying evaluative meaning and prepares for gap statements in research writing (Swales & Feak, 2012).

difficulties.pattern: Many research shows… / a lot of evidences.
difficulties.revealedBy: Count quantifiers with mass nouns and plural forms of mass nouns.
difficulties.response: Revisit countability and give matching quantifier sets (much, little, a great deal of, a large amount of with mass nouns; many, few, a number of with count nouns).

difficulties.pattern: Few and a few mean the same thing.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'A few' in gap statements or 'few' when listing supporting studies, producing the opposite of the intended claim.
difficulties.response: Use minimal pairs from real literature reviews and ask learners to state the writer's implied evaluation.

difficulties.pattern: Every students / each of the participant.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plural nouns after each and every, or singular nouns after 'each of the'.
difficulties.response: Contrast each/every + singular noun with each of + plural noun phrase, and note singular verb agreement in both.

diagnostic.task: Give the learner data showing that 3 of 40 studies found an effect and ask for one sentence presenting this as a gap and one presenting it as initial support.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses 'few' or 'only a small number of' for the gap and 'a few' or 'a small number of' for support, with correct countable nouns and agreement.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate grammar but no differentiation between the two framings.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Quantifier–noun mismatches or framings that contradict the data.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level the focus is countability matching and replacing informal quantifiers. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional teaching links quantifiers to describing data and to framing the literature.

guidance.summary: Corpus evidence shows that academic prose is dominated by present simple, with perfect and progressive aspect relatively infrequent (Biber et al., 1999). Teach tense through function in academic genres: generalisation and description of figures (present), completed procedures (past), and continuing relevance (present perfect), as treated in Swales and Feak (2012). Hinkel (2002) documents differences between L2 and L1 student writers in tense and aspect use, which supports explicit attention to genre-based tense choice.

activities.title: Tense mapping across sections
learnerActions: Highlight finite verbs in the introduction, methods and results of a short article in their field, using a different colour for each tense or aspect
Summarise the dominant tense in each section and explain why
Note any sentence that breaks the pattern and identify its function
activities.intendedInsight: Tense choices follow the function of each section and sentence, not a single rule for academic writing.
activities.rationale: Genre-based noticing of form–function patterns supports transfer to learners' own writing (Swales & Feak, 2012).

activities.title: Consistent tense in own paragraph
learnerActions: Mark every finite verb in a paragraph of own writing
Label each with its function (generalisation, completed action, continuing relevance)
Correct shifts that do not match a change of function
activities.intendedInsight: Unmotivated tense shifts confuse the reader about time and status.
activities.rationale: Linking tense to function in the learner's own text builds a self-editing routine that targets a rule-governed error type (Ferris, 1999).

difficulties.pattern: My teacher said academic writing always uses the present tense.
difficulties.revealedBy: Present tense used for the learner's own completed procedures or for specific past studies.
difficulties.response: Replace the single rule with function-based choices illustrated across sections of real articles.

difficulties.pattern: Writers whose first language marks time with adverbs rather than verb inflection may leave tense unmarked or inconsistent.
difficulties.revealedBy: Base forms or shifting tense within a paragraph where time is clear from context.
difficulties.response: Teach tense as an obligatory grammatical choice in English, then give a focused editing pass for finite verbs; if the learner cannot find the finite verb of each clause, return to clause analysis (grm.clause-elements).

difficulties.pattern: Present perfect means a short time ago.
difficulties.revealedBy: Present perfect with specific past time expressions (In 2015, Smith has found…).
difficulties.response: Contrast present perfect (no fixed past time; current relevance) with past simple (specific time or study), using citation examples.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a four-sentence paragraph that states a general fact about their field, reports what one study did, summarises research to date and describes a figure.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Present simple for the general fact and the figure, past for the specific study, present perfect for research to date, with consistent forms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most choices correct but one function mismatch, such as present perfect with a specific date.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Single tense throughout or frequent unmotivated shifts.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional UG learners need explicit control of forms and the main academic functions, and tense is assessed directly in their writing. Pre-sessional PG learners review it briefly and link tense to genre sections and literature-based writing. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners mainly need consistency and conventions for literature reviews and methods, usually through self-editing.

guidance.summary: Swales (1990) and Swales and Feak (2012) describe how tense in citing sentences signals the writer's stance towards cited work and correlates with citation form, and Shaw (1992) shows that tense, voice and reporting-verb choice correlate with the rhetorical function of the sentence. Hyland (1999) documents disciplinary variation in how sources are reported. Teach tense here as a rhetorical choice, using literature reviews from learners' own fields, rather than as a fixed rule.

activities.title: Tense and endorsement
learnerActions: Compare three versions of a citing sentence differing only in tense (Smith found / has found / finds that X)
Discuss what each implies about whether the finding still holds and whether the writer accepts it
Find two examples of each pattern in a literature review in their field
activities.intendedInsight: Tense in reporting can signal currency and generality, not just the date of publication; endorsement depends more on the reporting verb and on field conventions.
activities.rationale: Making the stance function of reporting tense explicit follows the account in Swales (1990) and Swales and Feak (2012) and supports more deliberate source use.

activities.title: Disciplinary tense audit
learnerActions: Collect 20 citing sentences from two recent articles in their field
Classify each by tense and by integral or non-integral citation
Write a short 'house style' note for their field and compare it with a peer from another discipline
activities.intendedInsight: Reporting conventions vary across disciplines, so the learner's field is the best guide.
activities.rationale: Hyland (1999) found clear disciplinary differences in citation practices; auditing one's own field builds autonomous genre awareness.

difficulties.pattern: The study was published in the past, so I must use past tense.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniform past tense in literature reviews, including for claims the writer clearly accepts as current.
difficulties.response: Show how present tense reporting of accepted claims and past tense reporting of specific procedures coexist in expert reviews; practise shifting between them.

difficulties.pattern: I change tense randomly when I cite.
difficulties.revealedBy: Mixed tenses in consecutive citing sentences with no change of function.
difficulties.response: Teach a default pattern for the learner's field and a small number of motivated departures, and check during editing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write three sentences reporting a single source: one describing what the researchers did, one presenting a finding they accept, and one summarising research in the area.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Past for procedure, present (or present perfect) for an accepted finding, present perfect for the area, with appropriate citation forms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct forms but no differentiation of the accepted finding, or inconsistent citation form.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Tense errors in form or random tense switching.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional UG courses introduce a default pattern for source-based essays. Pre-sessional PG courses teach reporting tense explicitly for the literature-based extended project. In-sessional PGT work, usually in literature-review sessions, has learners analyse their field's literature reviews; undergraduate in-sessional work does so where assignments are source-heavy. PGR writers need conscious control of tense to position their work in relation to others' findings.
reviewNotes: Disciplinary patterns in reporting tense are described in the literature as tendencies; learners should verify norms in their own target journals.

guidance.summary: The passive is markedly more frequent in academic prose than in other registers, and most academic passives omit the agent (Biber et al., 1999). Tarone et al. (1998) showed that astrophysics writers chose active and passive voice for rhetorical reasons, using 'we' with active verbs for their own choices, which counters the myth that the passive is simply 'objective'. Teach voice as a choice about topic continuity, agent relevance and authorial presence, with discipline norms on first person explicitly discussed (Hyland, 2002).

activities.title: Why passive here?
learnerActions: Identify every passive in a methods section and a discussion section in their field
For each, state why the agent is omitted or placed at the end, choosing from: unknown, obvious, irrelevant, keeping the topic as subject
Find any active 'we' sentences and explain why the writers chose them
activities.intendedInsight: Voice choices are made for information flow and rhetorical purpose, not to make text objective.
activities.rationale: Function-based analysis of voice in expert texts replicates the type of evidence in Tarone et al. (1998) and replaces prescriptive rules with genre-sensitive choices.

activities.title: Restoring agency
learnerActions: Take a paragraph of own writing with several passives
Mark any passive where the reader needs to know who acted (for example who proposed a claim or made a decision)
Rewrite those sentences actively and compare the paragraph's clarity
activities.intendedInsight: Unnecessary passives can hide responsibility and make argument harder to follow.
activities.rationale: Hyland (2002) shows that authorial presence is a rhetorical resource; deciding when to reveal agents builds control over it.

difficulties.pattern: I should always use the passive because it is objective.
difficulties.revealedBy: Uniformly passive texts, including passives that hide whose claim is being made.
difficulties.response: Present corpus and genre evidence, discuss discipline norms on 'we' and 'I', and practise justified voice choices. Do not replace one blanket rule with another.

difficulties.pattern: The problem was happened… / The results were arisen from…
difficulties.revealedBy: Passives formed with unaccusative intransitive verbs (happen, occur, arise, emerge, appear), whose subject undergoes rather than performs the event; this overpassivisation is attested across many first-language backgrounds and is largely developmental.
difficulties.response: Contrast transitive and intransitive verbs with examples, provide a short list of common academic intransitive verbs (occur, arise, emerge, happen), and contrast them with ergative verbs that work both ways (The temperature increased / The researchers increased the temperature; the rate changed / the dose was changed). The fuller treatment is in grm.unaccusative-verbs.

difficulties.pattern: Having analysed the data, it was found that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Dangling participles before passive main clauses.
difficulties.response: Teach the subject-sharing rule for introductory participle clauses and show active and passive repairs.

diagnostic.task: Give a five-sentence methods paragraph in active voice with 'the researcher' as subject in each sentence, and ask the learner to revise it for a journal in their field.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Varies voice for topic continuity, uses passive where the agent is obvious, and may use 'we' or retain active voice where the field expects it, with accurate verb forms.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Converts all sentences mechanically to passive with accurate forms but without considering flow or discipline norms.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Form errors in passive verb phrases or passives with intransitive verbs.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional UG learners need accurate forms and the main functions in process description and reports, and the passive is assessed directly. Pre-sessional PG and undergraduate in-sessional work addresses voice choice in reports, methods and essays. PGT and PGR writers should examine target-journal norms, including first-person active, and the interaction of voice with authorial stance.
reviewNotes: The edge from grm.clause-elements is partly implied via grm.tense-aspect (soft), but is kept because passivisation depends directly on identifying the object that becomes subject.

guidance.summary: Modal verbs are a frequent grammatical means of expressing tentativeness and inference in academic writing. Hyland's (1998) study of hedging in research articles shows that such devices serve both accuracy (fitting claims to evidence) and interpersonal purposes (anticipating readers' possible objections), and the Longman grammar documents how modal meanings and frequencies differ across registers (Biber et al., 1999). Teach epistemic meanings explicitly and in contrast with obligation and ability, using authentic discussion sections, and combine form work (modal + perfect, modal + passive) with judgements about claim strength. This topic covers the grammar of modals; the wider repertoire of hedging devices is treated in the stance domain.

activities.title: Ranking commitment
learnerActions: Read four versions of a claim about a set of results that differ only in the modal (may, might, could, must)
Rank them by strength of commitment and match each to a short description of evidence (one small study; several consistent studies; a strong logical inference)
Write a claim about their own field for weak, moderate and strong evidence
activities.intendedInsight: Modal choice should reflect the strength of the evidence and reasoning behind a claim.
activities.rationale: Hyland (1998) shows that hedging calibrates commitment to evidence; ranking makes the modal scale explicit before it is used.

activities.title: Modal meanings in discussion sections
learnerActions: Highlight all modal verbs in a discussion section from their field
Classify each as likelihood or inference, obligation or recommendation, or ability
Rewrite two likelihood sentences with a different modal and discuss how the claim changes
activities.intendedInsight: The same modal can express different meanings, and in discussion sections most modals express likelihood.
activities.rationale: Corpus descriptions show that modal meanings are distributed differently across registers (Biber et al., 1999), so classifying modals in context develops interpretive accuracy.

difficulties.pattern: Must means obligation, so 'this must be due to' sounds wrong to me.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misreading epistemic 'must' in sources as a rule or recommendation, or avoiding it entirely.
difficulties.response: Contrast epistemic and deontic uses with paired examples and show that epistemic 'must' signals strong inference from evidence.

difficulties.pattern: The results may possibly suggest that it might be…
difficulties.revealedBy: Stacked hedges that make the claim almost empty, often after instruction that stressed caution.
difficulties.response: Teach one well-chosen hedge per claim as a default and show expert examples. Do not discourage hedging itself.

difficulties.pattern: This may contributed to… / this could be caused (meaning a past cause).
difficulties.revealedBy: Form errors in modal + perfect and modal + passive, and present-time modals used for inferences about past events.
difficulties.response: Teach modal + have + past participle for past inference and modal + be + past participle for passive, with examples from discussion sections.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a sentence suggesting a possible cause of a past result, then to rank three modal versions of a claim and say which fits a described piece of weak evidence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses modal + perfect accurately for the past cause, ranks modals correctly and rejects 'must' for weak evidence with a reason.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct ranking but a form error in modal + perfect, or accurate form but uncertain ranking.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot distinguish strengths or confuses epistemic and deontic meanings.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need accurate modal forms and the main likelihood meanings. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional learners use modals to calibrate claims in essays and reports and to interpret claims in sources. At PGT level the focus is on discussion sections and on interpreting modal claims in research articles.

guidance.summary: Teach conditionals in academic writing as tools for stating the conditions under which a claim holds, for reasoning about alternatives and counterfactuals, and for describing dependencies in methods and models, rather than through the general-English 'zero to third' sequence. Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman (1999) emphasise meaning and use over formal types, and academic examples often combine tenses in ways the four-type scheme does not capture. Include the wider set of conditional subordinators (unless, provided that, assuming that, as long as) and conditional prepositional phrases (in the absence of, without).

activities.title: Qualifying a bold claim
learnerActions: Start with an unqualified generalisation from their field
Add conditions using if, unless and provided that, and one conditional prepositional phrase (in the absence of…)
Discuss in pairs which condition makes the claim most defensible and whether any condition changes the claim's meaning
activities.intendedInsight: Conditionals set the boundaries within which a claim is true.
activities.rationale: Focusing on meaning and use (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999) connects conditionals to argument and claim qualification rather than to imaginary situations.

activities.title: Counterfactual evaluation
learnerActions: Read a short case or study summary that turns on a key decision or design choice
Write two past unreal conditionals about what might have happened under a different decision
Evaluate which counterfactual is best supported by the evidence and express it with an appropriate modal
activities.intendedInsight: Counterfactual conditionals support causal reasoning and evaluation of decisions and designs.
activities.rationale: Using past unreal conditionals for evaluation shows how tense and modal choices encode hypothetical meaning (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999), a resource also needed in case-study and discussion writing.

difficulties.pattern: There are four conditionals and I must choose one of them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of mixed-time conditionals and of conditionals with modals other than will and would.
difficulties.response: Show authentic academic conditionals and teach the tense–meaning logic (real versus hypothetical, present versus past) rather than the four types.

difficulties.pattern: Unless the sample is large, the results are reliable.
difficulties.revealedBy: Conditions with reversed polarity after unless.
difficulties.response: Paraphrase unless as 'if … not' and ask learners to test each unless-sentence by rewriting it with if not.

difficulties.pattern: If the policy would be changed, unemployment would fall.
difficulties.revealedBy: Would in both clauses of hypothetical conditionals, in writers whose first languages mark hypothetical meaning in both clauses.
difficulties.response: Show that English marks hypothetical meaning with past forms in the if-clause and would in the main clause, and practise in short argument paragraphs.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to qualify a general claim (for example 'Raising the minimum wage reduces employment') with three different conditional forms or subordinators, one of them 'unless'.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Logically appropriate conditions, accurate tense and modal choices, and correct polarity with unless.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct forms but one illogical condition, or logic sound but one tense or modal error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Errors in both form and logic, or conditions that contradict the intended claim.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level, conditionals support reasoning in subject content and describing processes and dependencies. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work uses them for qualifying claims, evaluating alternatives and case-study reasoning.

guidance.summary: Relative clauses are a core postmodifying resource. In academic prose, 'which' occurs in both defining and non-defining clauses and preposition + which patterns (the extent to which; the conditions under which) are characteristic of formal writing (Biber et al., 1999). Teach the meaning difference between defining and non-defining clauses first, so that punctuation follows from meaning rather than from a memorised rule. Hinkel (2004) provides practical techniques for teaching relative clauses in academic writing, including combining and reduction tasks.

activities.title: Who was paid?
learnerActions: Compare sentence pairs that differ only in commas around the relative clause
Explain who or what is referred to in each version
Add one defining and one non-defining clause to a paragraph of own writing, punctuating each according to its meaning
activities.intendedInsight: Commas around relative clauses change what the sentence claims about a group of referents.
activities.rationale: Meaning-focused contrast makes punctuation a semantic decision rather than a memorised rule (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

activities.title: Preposition + which
learnerActions: Find examples such as 'the extent to which' and 'the theory on which' in a set text
Identify the verb, noun or adjective inside the relative clause that requires each preposition (rely on, extent to)
Combine sentence pairs from their own field using preposition + which, then compare with stranded-preposition versions and discuss register
activities.intendedInsight: The preposition before which comes from a word pattern inside the relative clause.
activities.rationale: Preposition + which patterns are frequent in formal academic prose (Biber et al., 1999) and are often avoided by learners; combining tasks are a practical way to build them (Hinkel, 2004).

difficulties.pattern: The method which we used it was effective.
difficulties.revealedBy: Resumptive pronouns inside relative clauses, in writers whose first languages allow or require a pronoun in the relativised position.
difficulties.response: Show that the relative pronoun takes the place of the noun inside the clause, and practise identifying and deleting the extra pronoun.

difficulties.pattern: Which always has commas; that never does.
difficulties.revealedBy: Commas around all which-clauses, including defining ones, or anxiety about using defining which at all.
difficulties.response: Focus on meaning: commas mark non-defining clauses whichever pronoun is used, and defining 'which' is common in British academic writing, though some US style guides prefer 'that'.

difficulties.pattern: The participants who their scores improved…
difficulties.revealedBy: Who + possessive instead of whose, or avoidance of whose with non-human antecedents (the theory of which the assumptions…).
difficulties.response: Teach whose as the possessive relative and show that it is acceptable with non-human antecedents in academic writing.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to combine three sentence pairs using relative clauses, one requiring preposition + which and one requiring whose, and to explain the meaning difference between a defining and non-defining version of one sentence.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate combinations, correct punctuation and a clear explanation of the meaning difference.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate combinations but an uncertain explanation, or a clear explanation but one punctuation or pronoun error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Resumptive pronouns, wrong relative pronouns or no understanding of the defining/non-defining distinction.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on form, pronoun choice and meaning in definitions and descriptions. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work focuses on preposition + which, whose and reduction to non-finite and prepositional postmodifiers.

guidance.summary: Non-finite clauses let writers add information without a full finite clause, and Biber et al. (2011) place non-finite postmodifiers among the later-developing phrasal features of academic writing. Teach them as reductions of finite clauses, working in both directions so that learners can parse them in reading and choose them in writing, and give explicit attention to the implied subject. Swales and Feak (2012) treat -ing clauses expressing result as a useful resource in explanation. Dangling participles are common in drafts and rarely block comprehension, but readers and editors notice them, so treat them as an editing target rather than a reason to avoid the structure.

activities.title: Reduction and expansion
learnerActions: Reduce five relative clauses from own writing to participle clauses, choosing -ing or -ed by active or passive meaning
Expand five participle and infinitive clauses from a set text back into finite clauses, supplying the subject and the logical relation (because, when, in order to, with the result that)
Discuss which reductions are possible, which lose information (for example tense) and which are ambiguous
activities.intendedInsight: Non-finite clauses are compressed finite clauses whose meaning depends on an implied subject, an implied relation and voice.
activities.rationale: Working in both directions links the form to its finite counterpart, supporting parsing as well as production; the Longman grammar documents the range of non-finite clause functions in academic prose (Biber et al., 1999).

activities.title: Dangling participle detective
learnerActions: Read eight sentences with introductory participle or infinitive clauses and say who performs the action in each
Mark sentences where the main-clause subject cannot be that performer
Repair each in two ways: change the main-clause subject (Having analysed the data, we found…) or expand the non-finite clause (After the data had been analysed, …)
Check own methods section for the same pattern
activities.intendedInsight: An introductory non-finite clause borrows its subject from the main clause, so the two must match.
activities.rationale: A clear rule plus repair practice suits a structure with a checkable rule (the implied subject must be the main-clause subject), although Ferris (1999) classed sentence-structure problems as less readily 'treatable' than agreement or tense, and applying it to the learner's own methods text builds an editing habit.

difficulties.pattern: Having collected the data, the results showed a clear trend.
difficulties.revealedBy: Dangling participles, especially before passive or inanimate main-clause subjects in methods and results sections.
difficulties.response: Teach the subject-sharing rule and the two repairs, noting conventional exceptions that are acceptable in academic prose (given…, considering…, assuming…, generally speaking…, compared with…) and that style guides disagree about 'Based on…'. Do not ban introductory participle clauses; they are useful and frequent in methods writing.

difficulties.pattern: The factors affected uptake were… / the data collecting in 2020.
difficulties.revealedBy: Wrong participle in reduced relatives, producing an unintended finite clause or the wrong voice.
difficulties.response: Return to the full relative clause, decide whether the head noun does or undergoes the action, then reduce.

difficulties.pattern: I use '-ing' clauses at the end of sentences to sound academic, but my tutor asks what I mean.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentence-final -ing clauses with an unclear relation or subject (Prices rose, causing concern among regulators being unable to…).
difficulties.response: Teach the result reading of sentence-final -ing clauses (thereby, thus + -ing) and ask writers to check that the whole preceding clause is the cause; replace with a finite clause where the relation is not result.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to rewrite a five-sentence methods paragraph using at least one to-infinitive clause of purpose, one reduced relative and one introductory participle clause.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All three structures are accurate, implied subjects match main-clause subjects, participle forms reflect voice and the paragraph is shorter without losing information.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Structures are present but there is one dangling participle or one wrong participle choice, which the learner can repair when it is pointed out.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Avoids non-finite clauses or produces several ungrammatical forms, such as finite verbs in reduced relatives.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional courses focus on reduced relatives and purpose clauses for methods and explanation, mainly in reading and controlled writing. Undergraduate in-sessional work addresses dangling participles and result clauses in lab and project reports. At PGT level the emphasis is on efficient, accurate use in dense methods and literature-review writing.

guidance.summary: Subordinators make logical relations explicit within a sentence, and concessive clauses in particular are a resource for stance: Chang and Schleppegrell (2011) argue for making such resources explicit to L2 writers. Corpus evidence, however, shows that finite adverbial clauses are more characteristic of conversation than of academic prose (Biber & Gray, 2010), so teaching should aim at accurate, logically precise subordination rather than at maximising the number of subordinate clauses. Teach subordinators alongside linking adverbials and prepositions with related meanings, because learners frequently confuse these word classes.

activities.title: Relation sort with three word classes
learnerActions: Sort a set of items (although, despite, however, because, because of, therefore, whereas, while, since) into subordinators, prepositions and linking adverbials
Write the same idea three ways (Although X, Y. / Despite X, Y. / X. However, Y.) for two relations
Note the punctuation and grammatical complement each form requires
activities.intendedInsight: The same logical relation can be expressed by different word classes that behave differently in the sentence.
activities.rationale: Explicit form–meaning–use contrasts support accurate choice among similar items (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

activities.title: Concede, then assert
learnerActions: Identify concessive sentences in a published argument and mark which clause carries the writer's own position
Write two concessive sentences about a debate in their field, putting the opposing view in the subordinate clause and their position in the main clause
Swap with a partner and check for double marking (although … but)
activities.intendedInsight: Concessive subordination lets writers acknowledge an alternative while keeping their own claim in the main clause.
activities.rationale: Chang and Schleppegrell (2011) show how explicit attention to such resources supports authorial stance in L2 academic writing.

difficulties.pattern: Although the results were positive, but the sample was small.
difficulties.revealedBy: Double marking of concession or reason (although … but; because … so), in writers whose first languages use paired connectives across both clauses.
difficulties.response: Show that English marks the relation once and practise removing the second marker; offer 'Although X, Y' and 'X, but Y' as alternatives.

difficulties.pattern: Because of the funding was reduced, …
difficulties.revealedBy: Clauses after prepositions (because of, despite, due to) and noun phrases after subordinators.
difficulties.response: Contrast clause complements and noun-phrase complements and practise expressing the same content both ways.

difficulties.pattern: While means 'during', so I do not use it for contrast.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misreading contrastive while and causal since in sources, or ambiguous use in writing.
difficulties.response: Show that while and since have temporal and logical meanings and that context, not the word alone, decides; advise whereas or because when ambiguity matters.

diagnostic.task: Give four pairs of clauses and ask the learner to combine each with a subordinator expressing a specified relation (concession, contrast, reason, purpose), then to rewrite one using a preposition instead.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct subordinators, no double marking, comma after initial subordinate clauses, and an accurate noun-phrase version with a preposition.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct relations but one double-marking, punctuation or preposition/subordinator confusion.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Wrong subordinators, fragments created by detached subordinate clauses, or no ability to rephrase with a preposition.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners need accurate subordinators and punctuation, often in explanation and cause–effect writing. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional teaching focuses on concession and contrast in argument and on the difference between subordinators and linking adverbials.

guidance.summary: Parallel structure is a clarity issue that becomes high-stakes in aims, research questions, lists and comparisons, and style manuals such as the APA Publication Manual (2020) treat parallel construction and seriation explicitly. Lu (2011) found that coordinate phrases per clause was among the measures that discriminated between proficiency levels, which suggests that phrasal coordination is part of developing academic writing rather than a basic skill. Teach parallelism through revision of learners' own lists and aims, and pair it with the ambiguity that coordination can create.

activities.title: Aims makeover
learnerActions: Write three aims or research questions for a real or planned project
Underline the first word of each and check whether all share one grammatical form
Revise for parallelism and compare with aims statements from published articles or dissertations in their field
activities.intendedInsight: Parallel form signals that items have equal status and makes lists faster to process.
activities.rationale: Revising authentic, high-stakes lists ties a grammatical principle to a genre need that style guides address directly (American Psychological Association, 2020).

activities.title: Correlatives and ambiguity
learnerActions: Find examples of not only … but also and both … and in a set text and mark the two parallel elements in each
Correct sentences with misplaced correlatives (The policy not only affects students but also staff)
Discuss ambiguous coordinations such as 'older men and women' and rewrite each to show both possible meanings
activities.intendedInsight: Correlatives must sit immediately before matching elements, and coordinated modifiers can be ambiguous about scope.
activities.rationale: Focused form practice suits rule-governed structures (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999), and ambiguity tasks show why the rule serves meaning.

difficulties.pattern: My list makes sense, so the form of each item does not matter.
difficulties.revealedBy: Lists that mix infinitives, -ing forms and noun phrases (to analyse, comparing and the evaluation of), especially in aims and bullet points.
difficulties.response: Add a parallelism check to the editing routine for every list, aim and heading set; highlight the first word of each item.

difficulties.pattern: Not only the results are important but also…
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentence-initial 'not only' without inversion, or correlatives placed before different types of constituent.
difficulties.response: Teach medial placement first (The results are not only X but also Y) and introduce initial placement with inversion later.

difficulties.pattern: I join everything with 'and'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Long chains of and-coordinated clauses that leave logical relations implicit.
difficulties.response: Show how subordination or a linking adverbial makes the relation explicit, and keep and-coordination for genuinely additive items.

diagnostic.task: Give three study aims in mixed forms and a sentence with a misplaced 'not only … but also'. Ask the learner to revise both and to explain the problem in each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Aims share one form, the correlatives precede matching constituents, and the explanation names parallel structure.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Fixes one problem but not the other, or fixes both without being able to explain why.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No improvement in parallelism or new errors introduced.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners work on lists, comparisons and correlatives. Undergraduate in-sessional work targets lists and headings in reports. At PGT level the priority is aims, objectives and research questions in proposals and dissertations.
reviewNotes: The point from Lu (2011) concerns a group-level measure that discriminated proficiency levels, not evidence that teaching phrasal coordination improves writing.

guidance.summary: That-clauses after verbs, adjectives and nouns are the main grammatical frame for reporting and evaluating propositions, and the Longman grammar shows that 'that' is usually retained in academic prose, whereas it is frequently omitted in conversation (Biber et al., 1999). Biber et al. (2011) place verb + finite complement clause early in their proposed developmental sequence, so most EAP learners already use it; teaching targets are embedded-question word order, noun complement clauses (the assumption that…) and the distinction between complementiser and relative 'that'.

activities.title: From questions to aims
learnerActions: Write three direct questions about a topic in their field
Rewrite each as an embedded clause in a statement of aims (This study examines whether/how…)
Check word order and choose between whether and if, noting that whether is preferred after prepositions and in formal writing
activities.intendedInsight: Embedded questions use statement word order and can carry the aims of a study.
activities.rationale: Converting direct questions into aims connects a known grammatical problem to a research-genre need (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

activities.title: Noun + that labels
learnerActions: Collect noun + that-clause examples from a set text (the assumption that, the view that, evidence that)
Classify the nouns as claims, beliefs, evidence or possibilities and note any evaluative meaning
Use three of them to label the positions in a short summary of a debate
activities.intendedInsight: Noun complement clauses let writers name and evaluate a proposition as a claim, a view or an assumption.
activities.rationale: Noun + that-clause structures are characteristic of written expository registers (Biber et al., 1999) and lead into stance and signalling-noun work.

difficulties.pattern: This study examines how does X affect Y.
difficulties.revealedBy: Question word order inside embedded clauses, particularly in aims and research questions.
difficulties.response: Contrast direct and embedded questions explicitly and practise in aims statements; check during editing.

difficulties.pattern: The finding that they reported it was surprising.
difficulties.revealedBy: Confusion between appositive that-clauses (complete) and relative clauses (with a gap), leading to resumptive pronouns or misreading.
difficulties.response: Show that an appositive that-clause is a complete proposition and can follow 'the fact', while a relative clause lacks an element and can take 'which'.

difficulties.pattern: I think the results show… (with 'that' dropped throughout an essay).
difficulties.revealedBy: Regular that-omission after reporting verbs in formal writing, carried over from speech.
difficulties.response: Point out that-omission as a feature of conversation and retain 'that' in formal writing, especially after reporting verbs separated from the clause.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write a three-sentence statement of aims containing two embedded questions and one noun + that-clause.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Statement word order, appropriate whether/how choice, 'that' retained, and an accurate noun complement clause.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One word-order error or one confusion of complementiser and relative 'that'.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Direct-question forms throughout or no complement clauses.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on reporting verb + that-clause and embedded questions. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work adds noun complement clauses for labelling and evaluating positions in source-based writing.

guidance.summary: Anticipatory-it frames such as 'it is important to' and 'it is possible that' are frequent lexical bundles in university registers (Biber, Conrad & Cortes, 2004), and Hunston and Sinclair's local grammar of evaluation, in Hunston and Thompson (2000), shows how the 'it + link verb + adjective + clause' pattern carries evaluation. Comparative work on student and published writing (Hewings & Hewings, 2002) reports differences in how often and for what purposes these frames are used. Teach them as stance resources, with explicit attention to frames that hide who holds a view and to frames that add words without adding stance.

activities.title: What stance does the frame carry?
learnerActions: Collect anticipatory-it sentences from a set text in their field
Classify the adjective, noun or verb in each frame by stance: likelihood, importance, clarity or obviousness, surprise, attribution
Write three sentences about their own topic using frames with different stances, and explain each choice to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: The adjective or verb inside the frame carries the writer's evaluation of the extraposed proposition.
activities.rationale: The local grammar of evaluation identifies this pattern as a central means of evaluation in English (Hunston & Thompson, 2000).

activities.title: Who argues this?
learnerActions: Find passive frames such as 'It is argued that' or 'It is believed that' in own writing
Decide in each case whether the reader needs to know who holds the view
Revise to name the source, to state the writer's own view, or keep the frame where the view is genuinely widespread
activities.intendedInsight: Passive anticipatory-it frames can obscure attribution, which affects both source use and voice.
activities.rationale: These frames are frequent in university registers (Biber et al., 2004), so learners need to control their attributional effect, not only their form.

difficulties.pattern: It is important to note that… begins half my paragraphs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated frames that add length without a distinct stance, often learned as set phrases.
difficulties.response: Show alternatives (an evaluative adverb, a direct statement) and practise deleting frames that add nothing. Do not ban the structure, which is frequent in expert writing.

difficulties.pattern: Is important to note that… / Is clear that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Omitted dummy subject, in writers whose first languages allow subjectless clauses.
difficulties.response: Show that English finite clauses require a subject, and that 'it' fills the subject slot when the real subject is extraposed.

difficulties.pattern: It is believed that this policy failed (but I cannot say by whom).
difficulties.revealedBy: Unattributed passive frames in source-based writing that a marker queries.
difficulties.response: Link the frame to attribution: either cite the holders of the view or present it as the writer's own judgement.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to write three sentences about a debate in their field using anticipatory-it frames with clearly different stances, and to revise one given unattributed frame.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate frames with differentiated stance, appropriate clause types, and a revision that restores attribution.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate forms but similar stance in each sentence, or a revision that simply deletes the frame.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Missing dummy subject, wrong clause type after the frame, or no awareness of the attribution problem.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on accurate forms with common adjectives. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work focuses on stance and attribution in source-based writing. At PGT level the emphasis is on economy and on matching frames to the strength of claims.

guidance.summary: Existential there + be postpones a new entity to the position after the verb, in line with the given-before-new tendency of English clauses (Biber et al., 1999). In academic writing it frames evidence, developments, gaps and enumerations (there is little evidence that; there has been a shift towards; there are three reasons for). Teach it with these academic functions, with notional-subject agreement, and with explicit repair of the frequent error of following it directly with a second finite verb. Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman (1999) stress its discourse function of introducing new information.

activities.title: Introducing evidence, change and gaps
learnerActions: Find existential-there sentences in a literature review or introduction from their field
Classify each by function: introducing evidence, signalling change, indicating a gap or enumerating
Write one sentence for each function about their own topic, using present, past or present perfect forms of be
activities.intendedInsight: Existential there is a frame for introducing new evidence, developments and gaps, not a general sentence opener.
activities.rationale: Function-focused analysis links the structure to its discourse role of presenting new information (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

activities.title: Repairing the double verb
learnerActions: Look at sentences such as 'There are many studies show that…'
Repair each in two ways: insert a relative pronoun (There are many studies that show…) or delete the frame (Many studies show…)
Decide which repair is more concise or better suited to the paragraph and explain why
activities.intendedInsight: Existential there cannot be followed directly by a second finite verb, and deleting the frame is often the better repair.
activities.rationale: Targeted repair of a frequent, recognisable error pattern supports self-editing; Ferris (1999) would class this sentence-structure error as less readily 'treatable' than agreement or tense, so expect repeated practice to be needed.

difficulties.pattern: There are many people think that…
difficulties.revealedBy: A second finite verb directly after existential there, in writers whose first languages allow an existential phrase to be followed directly by a predicate.
difficulties.response: Teach the relative-clause and deletion repairs and add the pattern to the learner's editing checklist.

difficulties.pattern: There have a debate about…
difficulties.revealedBy: Use of 'have' instead of 'be', in writers whose first languages express existence with a verb meaning 'have'.
difficulties.response: Contrast existential be with possessive have, and show that 'there have been' is the present perfect of be, not a use of possessive have.

difficulties.pattern: There is many factors that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Singular be with a plural notional subject, often in speech-influenced writing.
difficulties.response: Show that be agrees with the noun phrase after it in formal writing, while noting that 'there's' + plural is common in speech.

diagnostic.task: Give three erroneous sentences (There are many studies show…; There have a debate…; There is many factors…) and ask the learner to correct them and then write two new existential sentences about their field.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All three repaired, with deletion of the frame chosen where it is more concise; new sentences use agreement and tense accurately for academic functions.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Two of three repaired, or repairs correct but new sentences use the frame as a generic opener.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Errors persist or new errors appear.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on form, agreement and the double-verb repair. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work focuses on evidence and gap statements in introductions and literature reviews.

guidance.summary: Comparison is central to data commentary, compare–contrast writing and evaluation, and Swales and Feak (2012) treat data commentary as a genre in which comparison and qualification are central. The Longman grammar describes the range of comparative forms and degree modifiers (Biber et al., 1999). Teach comparison with real data so that degree modifiers can be calibrated to actual differences, and give explicit attention to logical comparison (comparing like with like) and to multiplicative expressions, which are a frequent source of ambiguity.

activities.title: Calibrating comparisons to data
learnerActions: Look at a table with values for three groups or years
Write sentences using degree modifiers (slightly, considerably, markedly) and one multiplicative comparison (twice as high as)
Swap with a partner and check that each modifier matches the size of the difference and each multiplicative is arithmetically correct
activities.intendedInsight: Comparative language makes quantitative claims that must match the data.
activities.rationale: Data commentary requires precise and qualified comparison (Swales & Feak, 2012).

activities.title: Comparing like with like
learnerActions: Identify illogical comparisons in sample sentences (The unemployment rate in Spain is higher than Germany)
Repair them with that of / those of or by repeating the head noun
Write three comparisons from a dataset in their own field and check each for logic
activities.intendedInsight: A comparison must set equivalent categories side by side.
activities.rationale: Logical comparison is rule-governed and therefore suited to explicit teaching and self-checking (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

difficulties.pattern: The salary of nurses is lower than doctors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comparisons between non-equivalent categories, especially in data commentary.
difficulties.response: Teach that of / those of and the parallelism principle behind them, and add a logic check to editing.

difficulties.pattern: Three times higher than and three times as high as mean the same.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ambiguous or arithmetically wrong multiplicative comparisons, and inconsistent use of 'per cent' versus 'percentage points'.
difficulties.response: Show the arithmetic behind each form, recommend 'three times as high as' or a stated ratio where precision matters, and link to relative and absolute change.

difficulties.pattern: More higher / the most largest.
difficulties.revealedBy: Double comparatives and superlatives.
difficulties.response: Contrast inflected and periphrastic comparatives and give a short rule by syllable length with academic examples.

diagnostic.task: Give a small table with values for three groups and ask the learner to write four comparative sentences, including one multiplicative comparison and one using that of / those of.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate forms, logically equivalent comparisons, correct multiplicative, and degree modifiers that fit the data.
