diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate forms but one illogical comparison or one modifier that over- or under-states the difference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Several form errors, illogical comparisons or arithmetic errors.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on comparative forms and simple data description. Pre-sessional and undergraduate in-sessional work focuses on data commentary and compare–contrast writing with precise degree modifiers.

guidance.summary: Prepositions in academic writing are largely governed by the words they follow, so they are best learned as parts of lexico-grammatical patterns (Hunston, 2002) rather than inferred from spatial meaning. Complex prepositions such as in terms of, with respect to and as a result of are characteristic of written academic registers (Biber et al., 1999). Corpus consultation is an efficient way for learners to check uncertain combinations (Boulton & Cobb, 2017). Treat prescriptive debates, such as 'due to' as an adverbial, as style-guide variation rather than error.

activities.title: Building a pattern list
learnerActions: Collect 20 academic verbs, nouns and adjectives with their dependent prepositions from set texts (focus on, impact on, consistent with, the relationship between)
Organise them by head word and add one example sentence from the source
Test a partner by giving the head word and asking for the preposition and an example
activities.intendedInsight: Dependent prepositions belong to the word that precedes them and are learned as patterns.
activities.rationale: Pattern grammar treats such combinations as units of form and meaning (Hunston, 2002), which supports learning them as chunks.

activities.title: Corpus check
learnerActions: Choose a head noun they are unsure about (impact, effect, influence)
Search an academic corpus for the noun followed by each candidate preposition
Compare frequencies and meanings and decide which to use in their own writing
activities.intendedInsight: Corpus evidence resolves many preposition doubts faster than rules.
activities.rationale: A meta-analysis of data-driven learning reports positive effects of corpus use on learning (Boulton & Cobb, 2017).

difficulties.pattern: We will discuss about this issue / emphasise on the role of…
difficulties.revealedBy: Prepositions added after transitive verbs whose translation equivalents in the first language take a preposition, or after nouns (discussion about) carried over to the verb.
difficulties.response: Highlight common academic verbs that take a direct object (discuss, emphasise, approach, address) and contrast them with their noun forms (a discussion of, an emphasis on).

difficulties.pattern: In terms of is a useful general linking phrase.
difficulties.revealedBy: Repeated 'in terms of' with no clear dimension or respect being specified.
difficulties.response: Show its specific meaning (with respect to a dimension) and offer more precise alternatives for the relation intended.

difficulties.pattern: Prepositions have meanings, so I work them out logically.
difficulties.revealedBy: Plausible but non-standard choices (an increase of 10% in X used for 'an increase in X of 10%') and inconsistency across drafts.
difficulties.response: Explain that many dependent prepositions are conventional rather than predictable, and shift the learner to pattern lists and corpus checks.

diagnostic.task: Give eight sentences with prepositions removed after common academic verbs, nouns and adjectives, plus two sentences requiring a complex preposition. Ask the learner to complete them and say how they would check two they were unsure about.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Nearly all prepositions correct and a concrete checking strategy (learner dictionary example sentences, corpus search).
diagnostic.partialResponse: Several errors but a sensible checking strategy, or accurate answers but no strategy.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Frequent errors and reliance on guessing.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on frequent dependent prepositions in their subject areas. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners add complex prepositions, corpus or dictionary checking routines and awareness of style-guide variation.

guidance.summary: Clefts are information-structure resources that divide a proposition so that one element is placed in focus. Functional grammars describe it-clefts as predicated theme and wh-clefts as a type of thematic equative (Thompson, 2014; Halliday & Matthiessen, 2014), and corpus evidence shows that both are marked, comparatively infrequent choices (Biber et al., 1999). Teach clefts as tools for contrast, correction and foregrounding a conclusion, not as general emphasis, and distinguish it-clefts from anticipatory-it extraposition.

activities.title: Correcting an assumption
learnerActions: Read a short paragraph that sets up a common assumption about a topic in their field
Write an it-cleft that corrects it (It is not X but Y that…)
Compare with a non-cleft version and discuss what the cleft presupposes and where it directs the reader's attention
activities.intendedInsight: It-clefts put contrastive focus on one element against a presupposed background.
activities.rationale: Functional descriptions of predicated theme explain the focusing effect and its link to presupposition (Thompson, 2014).

activities.title: Cleft or extraposition?
learnerActions: Sort ten sentences beginning 'It is…' into clefts and extraposition
Apply the test: can the sentence be rewritten as a plain clause by removing 'It is… that'?
Write one cleft and one extraposed sentence about the same finding
activities.intendedInsight: Clefts and extraposition share a surface form but do different work.
activities.rationale: Contrasting similar forms reduces confusion, and the Longman grammar describes both structures and their distribution (Biber et al., 1999).

difficulties.pattern: Clefts make my points stronger, so I use them often.
difficulties.revealedBy: Several clefts per page without any contrast or correction, producing an emphatic, speech-like tone.
difficulties.response: Limit clefts to points of genuine contrast or to signalling a main conclusion, and show unmarked alternatives.

difficulties.pattern: It is clear that the method that matters.
difficulties.revealedBy: Blends of cleft and extraposition, or misreading clefts in sources as evaluative statements.
difficulties.response: Use the rewriting test and contrast pairs.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph that sets up an assumption and ask the learner to write an it-cleft correcting it and a wh-cleft stating the conclusion; then ask them to identify which of two 'It is…' sentences is a cleft.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate clefts with a clear contrastive purpose and correct identification with a reason.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate forms but weak contrastive purpose, or correct forms but misidentification.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Ungrammatical clefts or no understanding of the difference from extraposition.

guidance.contextNotes: On pre-sessional courses clefts are mainly a reading point for higher-level learners. Undergraduate, PGT and PGR writers use them to mark contrast with previous research and to foreground conclusions in discussion sections.

guidance.summary: Fronting and inversion are marked word orders; the Longman grammar shows them to be comparatively infrequent but functional, typically linking a fronted element to preceding discourse or creating contrast (Biber et al., 1999). In functional terms they create marked themes (Thompson, 2014; Halliday & Matthiessen, 2014). Teach them mainly for comprehension of formal prose and for occasional, motivated use, rather than as a way of 'sounding advanced'.

activities.title: Why is this fronted?
learnerActions: Find fronted structures in a set text (Of particular concern is…; Central to this argument is…)
Explain how the fronted element links to the previous sentence and where the new information ends up
Rewrite each in canonical order and judge which version reads more smoothly in context
activities.intendedInsight: Fronting is motivated by information flow: it puts linking material first and heavy new material last.
activities.rationale: Marked theme choices link clauses to their discourse context (Thompson, 2014).

activities.title: Operator practice in context
learnerActions: Rewrite sentences with 'Not only', 'Only when' and 'Rarely' using inversion
Check that the operator matches the tense and aspect of the original verb
Decide in pairs which rewritten versions are appropriate in context and which sound mannered
activities.intendedInsight: Inversion requires the correct operator and should be reserved for genuine emphasis or contrast.
activities.rationale: Focused form practice suits a rule-governed structure, while the appropriateness discussion reflects its low frequency in academic prose (Biber et al., 1999).

difficulties.pattern: Not only the results show… but also…
difficulties.revealedBy: Missing operator after fronted negative or restrictive elements.
difficulties.response: Teach operator insertion (do/does/did, has, can) and show the medial alternative that needs no inversion.

difficulties.pattern: Inversion sounds impressive, so I use it to start paragraphs.
difficulties.revealedBy: Several inversions in a short text with no link to preceding discourse.
difficulties.response: Limit to cases where the fronted element links back or marks contrast, and show how overuse affects tone.

diagnostic.task: Give a context sentence and three follow-up sentences; ask the learner to rewrite one with a fronted complement and inversion and one with 'Not only', and to explain why the third should stay in canonical order.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Accurate operators and word order, fronted elements that link to the context, and a reasoned choice to keep one sentence canonical.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Accurate forms but no discourse motivation, or motivation explained but one form error.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Inaccurate forms or no understanding of why fronting is used.

guidance.contextNotes: Undergraduate in-sessional learners mainly need to parse fronted structures in reading. PGT and PGR writers may use them occasionally for linking and contrast in discussions and theoretical writing.

guidance.summary: Linking adverbials are particularly frequent in academic prose; the Longman grammar reports that initial position is the most common overall, while medial position is comparatively frequent in academic writing (Biber et al., 1999). Learner corpus research reports mismatches with expert usage, including over- and under-use of particular connectors and a preference for sentence-initial placement (Granger, 1998; Granger & Tyson, 1996). Teach placement and punctuation together, with the comma splice (…, however, …) as the key accuracy target and medial placement as a range target.

activities.title: Position audit
learnerActions: Highlight every linking adverbial in a published article from their field and in an equivalent stretch of their own writing
Record the position of each (initial, medial, final) and the punctuation used
Compare the two distributions and move two of their own connectors to medial position, checking the result reads naturally
activities.intendedInsight: Expert writers vary connector position, and medial placement can put the preceding element in focus.
activities.rationale: Comparing learner and expert texts is the core method of learner corpus research and makes distributional differences visible (Granger, 1998).

activities.title: Splice repair
learnerActions: Identify comma splices with however, therefore and moreover in a paragraph
Repair each with a semicolon, a full stop or a conjunction (but, so)
Explain to a partner why 'but' can join two clauses with a comma and 'however' cannot
activities.intendedInsight: Linking adverbials link sentences; they do not join clauses.
activities.rationale: The comma splice with linking adverbials follows a clear punctuation rule and suits focused self-editing; Ferris (1999) listed fragments, not comma splices, among 'treatable' errors, so the extension is by analogy.

difficulties.pattern: X is important, however, Y is also important.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comma splices with linking adverbials, often alongside correct use of 'but'.
difficulties.response: Contrast conjunctions and linking adverbials as word classes and give the three repair options.

difficulties.pattern: Every new sentence needs a connector at the start.
difficulties.revealedBy: Connector-initial sentences throughout, often from writing-test preparation that rewarded visible linking.
difficulties.response: Show expert paragraphs where many sentences have no connector and cohesion comes from reference and given–new ordering; practise medial placement and deletion.

difficulties.pattern: The results, however, were mixed — I put commas everywhere around connectors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Commas around every connector, including those that are usually unpunctuated in medial position (thus, therefore after an auxiliary).
difficulties.response: Show that commas around medial connectors are often optional and that style guides vary; aim for consistency rather than one rule.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with five linking adverbials, all sentence-initial, including two comma splices. Ask the learner to repair the splices and move two adverbials to medial position.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Both splices repaired correctly; medial adverbials placed after the subject or first auxiliary and punctuated consistently.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Splices repaired but medial placement ungrammatical, or placement correct but one splice remains.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Splices persist and the learner cannot explain the difference between however and but.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners focus on the splice repair and the conjunction/adverbial distinction. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional work focuses on reducing sentence-initial connectors and using medial placement in extended writing.
reviewNotes: The positional claim (initial position most frequent overall; medial position comparatively frequent in academic prose) is summarised from the Longman grammar (Biber et al., 1999) as a tendency, not as a frequency ranking for every connector.

guidance.summary: Reporting structures are the grammar of attribution. Thompson and Tribble (2001) distinguish integral citations (verb-controlling, naming, non-citation) from non-integral ones and use corpus data to show how these vary, which provides a practical framework for teaching reporting patterns. Thompson and Ye (1991) and Hyland (1999) show that reporting verbs carry evaluation and vary by discipline. This topic focuses on the grammar of the frames; choosing verbs for their evaluative force is treated under source use.

activities.title: Pattern sort
learnerActions: Collect 15 reporting sentences from a set text
Sort them by pattern: verb + that-clause, verb + noun phrase, verb + noun + as, verb + wh-clause, passive or raising, adjunct (according to, as X notes)
Write one new sentence about a source they know for each pattern
activities.intendedInsight: Reporting relies on a small set of grammatical patterns, each with its own constraints.
activities.rationale: Thompson and Tribble's (2001) corpus-based typology of citation supports systematic, pattern-based teaching.

activities.title: Repair the frame
learnerActions: Identify errors such as 'According to Smith, he argues that…' and 'Jones described the policy is a failure'
Repair each and name the problem (double attribution, wrong complementation)
Check the reporting sentences in their own latest draft for the same problems
activities.intendedInsight: Adjunct frames and verb frames should not be combined, and each reporting verb has its own pattern.
activities.rationale: Reporting-frame errors are largely lexically governed (each verb has its own complementation), so they are best tracked verb by verb in a personal pattern record and checked against a corpus or learner dictionary.

difficulties.pattern: According to Smith, he argues that…
difficulties.revealedBy: Double attribution combining an adjunct frame with a reporting verb and a pronoun subject.
difficulties.response: Contrast the two frames and practise converting between them; check in editing.

difficulties.pattern: Smith discussed about the problem / Jones described it is a failure.
difficulties.revealedBy: Complementation errors where the translation equivalent of the verb takes a different pattern in the first language.
difficulties.response: Teach each high-frequency reporting verb with its pattern and an example, and encourage dictionary or corpus checks for new verbs.

difficulties.pattern: I always use 'X said that'.
difficulties.revealedBy: One reporting frame repeated throughout a source-based essay.
difficulties.response: Show the range of integral and non-integral patterns and how varying them also varies prominence of author versus information.

diagnostic.task: Give five erroneous reporting sentences and ask the learner to correct them, then write two reporting sentences about a source they know using different patterns.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All errors repaired with accurate complementation, and two different, accurate patterns in the new sentences.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most errors repaired but one double attribution or complementation error remains, or new sentences use the same pattern.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Errors persist and the learner cannot explain them.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners focus on accurate core patterns in summaries and source-based essays. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners extend to passive and raising patterns and to varying prominence in literature reviews.

guidance.summary: Reference is one of the core cohesive resources identified by Halliday and Hasan (1976), and ambiguous pronouns and demonstratives are a frequent clarity problem in student writing. Swales and Feak (2012) recommend 'this + summary noun' when a demonstrative refers back to a stretch of text. Chang and Swales (1999), however, show that style-manual prohibitions on 'unattended' this do not reflect all expert practice, so present the noun as a clarity strategy for ambiguous cases rather than as an absolute rule.

activities.title: Antecedent arrows
learnerActions: Mark every pronoun and demonstrative in a paragraph of own writing
Draw an arrow to its antecedent and circle any case where there are two or more candidates, or where the antecedent is a whole clause
Revise only the circled cases, by adding a noun, repeating the key term or restructuring
activities.intendedInsight: Every pronoun needs one recoverable antecedent; the problem is ambiguity, not pronouns as such.
activities.rationale: Reference ties are central to cohesion (Halliday & Hasan, 1976), and making the ties visible lets writers see what a reader must infer.

activities.title: Choosing the summary noun
learnerActions: Find 'this' or 'these' used without a noun in a set text and in own writing
Propose a summarising noun for each (this finding, this assumption, these limitations) and discuss whether it evaluates as well as labels
Decide which cases were clear without a noun and which needed one
activities.intendedInsight: A summary noun clarifies reference and also characterises what is being referred to.
activities.rationale: Swales and Feak (2012) recommend this strategy, and the evaluation discussion links it to signalling nouns (Flowerdew, 2003).

difficulties.pattern: This shows that… (and the reader cannot tell what 'this' is).
difficulties.revealedBy: Demonstratives referring vaguely to a previous paragraph or to several possible propositions; tutors' marginal 'what does this refer to?'.
difficulties.response: Add a summary noun in ambiguous cases. Do not impose a blanket ban on 'this' as a pronoun.

difficulties.pattern: These criterion… / this phenomena… / these data shows… (plural data with a singular verb).
difficulties.revealedBy: Number mismatches between demonstratives and nouns with irregular or Latinate plurals.
difficulties.response: Check irregular plurals and agree on a consistent policy for 'data'.

difficulties.pattern: I avoid pronouns and repeat the full noun every time to be safe.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy repetition of long noun phrases that makes text laborious, often after negative feedback on ambiguity.
difficulties.response: Reassure that clear pronouns are expected and show how reference chains mix pronouns, demonstratives and repeated key terms.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with three ambiguous pronouns or demonstratives and ask the learner to list all possible antecedents for each and revise.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Detects every ambiguity, revises with accurate summary nouns or restructuring, and leaves clear pronouns untouched.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Detects most ambiguities but revises by repeating long noun phrases, or chooses an inaccurate summary noun.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not detect the ambiguity or replaces every pronoun indiscriminately.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners focus on clear antecedents and number agreement. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners work on summary nouns and on reference across paragraph boundaries in extended writing.
reviewNotes: Chang and Swales (1999) include unattended anaphoric 'this' among the ten informal features they examined; Gray and Cortes (2011) also document unattended this/these in published prose.

guidance.summary: Substitution and ellipsis are cohesive ties alongside reference (Halliday & Hasan, 1976), and in academic writing their most important uses are 'that of / those of' in comparisons and 'do so' or ellipsis to avoid repeating verb phrases. Teach them with attention to recoverability and number agreement, and balance them against the expectation of terminological consistency: repeating a key term is often clearer than substituting for it.

activities.title: Reducing repetition without losing meaning
learnerActions: Identify repeated noun phrases and verb phrases in a paragraph of own writing
Revise using one/ones, that of/those of, do so or ellipsis
Ask a partner to say what each substitute stands for, and restore the original wording where they cannot
activities.intendedInsight: Substitution and ellipsis reduce repetition only when the reader can recover what has been left out.
activities.rationale: Substitution and ellipsis are described as cohesive ties that depend on a recoverable presupposed element (Halliday & Hasan, 1976).

activities.title: Making comparisons logical
learnerActions: Repair illogical comparisons in data-commentary sentences with that of / those of
Check number agreement between the substitute and the noun it replaces
Write two comparisons from a table in their field using the structure
activities.intendedInsight: That of and those of let a writer compare equivalent things without repeating the head noun.
activities.rationale: The structure is rule-governed and frequent in academic comparisons (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

difficulties.pattern: The results of this study are similar to that of Smith.
difficulties.revealedBy: Number mismatch between that/those and the head noun replaced.
difficulties.response: Teach the agreement check and practise with plural and uncountable heads.

difficulties.pattern: Repeating words is bad style, so I replace them every time.
difficulties.revealedBy: Substitutes or synonyms used for key technical terms, creating doubt about whether the same referent is meant.
difficulties.response: Distinguish key terms, which should be repeated, from incidental repetition, which can be reduced; link to terminological consistency.

difficulties.pattern: One for everything: the information and the one from the survey.
difficulties.revealedBy: 'One/ones' used to substitute uncountable nouns.
difficulties.response: Show that one/ones replace countable nouns and that uncountable nouns need that of, repetition or ellipsis.

diagnostic.task: Give a paragraph with repetitive structures and an illogical comparison (The salary of nurses is lower than doctors) and ask the learner to revise it.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Comparison made logical with correct number, verb-phrase repetition reduced, and key terms retained.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Comparison fixed but substitution introduces ambiguity, or repetition reduced but the comparison remains illogical.
diagnostic.gapResponse: No meaningful revision or new errors introduced.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners focus on that of / those of in data commentary. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners use substitution and ellipsis for concision, balancing it against terminological consistency.

guidance.summary: Error monitoring is a self-regulatory strategy (Zimmerman, 2002) through which learners turn feedback into targeted editing. Ferris (1999) distinguishes 'treatable' rule-governed errors (agreement, verb forms, articles, fragments) from less rule-governed lexical ones, and Bitchener and Ferris (2012) discuss error logs and focused self-editing; meta-analytic evidence suggests written corrective feedback can improve accuracy (Kang & Han, 2015), though the debate initiated by Truscott (1996) shows that effects depend on how feedback is used. Ellis and Yuan (2004) found that careful online planning was associated with greater accuracy, which is consistent with, though it did not test, separating composing from monitoring.

activities.title: Error log built from your own feedback
learnerActions: Go through feedback on two or three recent assignments and record each grammatical error with its type, the original sentence and a correction
Count types and choose three to five priorities, favouring frequent, treatable errors that affect meaning or reader judgement
For each priority, write a one-line rule or check question in own words
activities.intendedInsight: Each writer's errors cluster into a small number of personal patterns that can be targeted.
activities.rationale: Error logs and prioritisation of treatable errors are recommended in the written corrective feedback literature (Bitchener & Ferris, 2012; Ferris, 1999).

activities.title: Single-focus editing passes
learnerActions: Edit a new draft in separate passes, one for each priority error type, using a search or highlighting strategy (for example, highlight every main verb for agreement)
Compare the number of errors found with a single general read-through of another paragraph
Reflect on which passes found most errors and adjust the routine
activities.intendedInsight: Monitoring for one feature at a time catches errors that a general read-through misses.
activities.rationale: Accuracy benefits from time and attention for careful monitoring (Ellis & Yuan, 2004), and focused passes direct that attention.

difficulties.pattern: I read my essay once at the end and I do not see any errors.
difficulties.revealedBy: Errors of types the learner can correct when they are pointed out remain in submitted work.
difficulties.response: Teach single-focus passes, reading aloud and a time gap between drafting and editing. Do not respond by re-teaching rules the learner already knows.

difficulties.pattern: My feedback is full of codes and I do not know what to do with them.
difficulties.revealedBy: Feedback returned unread or corrections made only where a direct correction was given.
difficulties.response: Work through the correction code with the learner's own feedback and model converting it into log entries.

difficulties.pattern: There are too many errors; I will never be accurate.
difficulties.revealedBy: Discouragement after heavily marked drafts, avoidance of editing or of complex structures.
difficulties.response: Narrow focus to a few high-impact priorities, show progress across drafts with the log, and frame some errors as evidence of attempting new structures.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to bring two marked pieces of writing, identify their three most frequent error types with examples, and then edit a new paragraph for those types only.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Priorities grounded in counted evidence, a stated check for each, and most target errors found in the new paragraph.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Plausible priorities but not evidence-based, or an editing pass that catches only some target errors.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot name priorities, or names generic categories ('grammar', 'vocabulary') without examples.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners are introduced to correction codes and simple logs. Pre-sessional courses build the routine into drafting cycles for the progression assignment. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners apply it independently to assessed work. PGR writers use it for publication-ready accuracy, alongside permitted proofreading and literacy brokers.
reviewNotes: The effectiveness of written corrective feedback remains debated (Truscott, 1996; Ferris, 1999; Kang & Han, 2015); the activities are proposals for using feedback, not claims that a particular procedure has been tested.

guidance.summary: Corpus grammars show that conversation differs systematically from academic writing: it relies on clause chaining, situational ellipsis, prefaces and tags (often taught as heads and tails), discourse markers and vague expressions, and it elaborates meaning through clauses rather than compressed noun phrases (Biber et al., 1999; Halliday, 1989). University speech such as classroom teaching and study groups shares many of these features (Biber, 2006), and vague language does interpersonal work rather than simply signalling imprecision (Channell, 1994). Teach spoken grammar as a set of resources with their own norms, and set accuracy priorities for speech by asking what affects understanding rather than by applying written-grammar correction to talk.

activities.title: What does speech do differently?
learnerActions: Read or listen to a short study-group or seminar exchange and mark heads, tails, ellipsis, discourse markers and vague expressions
For each feature, say what it does for the listener (introduces a topic, clarifies a referent, saves repetition, softens a claim)
Rewrite two turns as they would appear in a written summary and compare what changed
activities.intendedInsight: Spoken grammar is organised for real-time listening and interaction, so features that would be edited out of writing do useful work in speech.
activities.rationale: Contrasting spoken and written versions of the same content makes the register differences described in corpus and functional grammars visible (Biber et al., 1999; Halliday, 1989).

activities.title: Accuracy priorities for speaking
learnerActions: Record a one- to two-minute answer to a seminar question and transcribe it, or check an automatic transcript
Mark only features that could cause misunderstanding (a verb form that changes time or certainty, missing negation, an unclear it or this) and leave features that are normal in speech
Record the answer again with attention to one priority feature
activities.intendedInsight: In speech some accuracy features carry meaning and others do not, so monitoring effort is better spent on the former.
activities.rationale: University spoken registers differ from writing in their grammatical profile (Biber, 2006), so correcting speech against written norms misdirects attention; the prioritisation step is a proposal intended to focus monitoring on meaning-bearing features, not a tested procedure.

difficulties.pattern: I should speak in full, correct sentences, like in my essays.
difficulties.revealedBy: Slow, heavily planned contributions that sound like written text read aloud, late entry into discussion, or self-interruptions to repair features that are normal in speech.
difficulties.response: Show transcripts of proficient academic speakers, including users of English as an additional language, using ellipsis, heads and tails and discourse markers, and practise short elliptical responses. Do not present spoken features as a lower standard or as permission to ignore errors that affect meaning.

difficulties.pattern: If I say 'sort of' or 'and things like that', I sound as if I don't know the answer.
difficulties.revealedBy: Either no vague expressions at all, giving blunt or over-precise statements, or heavy reliance on them in place of content when explaining a concept.
difficulties.response: Discuss what vague expressions do (approximating, appealing to shared knowledge, softening) and practise replacing them with specific content where the listener needs precision.

difficulties.pattern: My tutor corrects my grammar every time I speak in the seminar, so I have stopped talking.
difficulties.revealedBy: Reduced participation after public correction of features that did not impede understanding, or speaking assessments that apply written-grammar criteria to spoken performance.
difficulties.response: For teachers and assessors: separate feedback on errors that affect meaning from features that are normal in speech, give accuracy feedback privately or after the discussion, and check that speaking criteria credit effective spoken grammar. For learners: ask for feedback focused on the features that affect understanding.

diagnostic.task: Give a 90-second transcript of a study-group exchange and ask the learner which three features would change in a written summary and why; then ask them to answer a discussion question orally for one minute.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Identifies heads, tails, ellipsis or vague markers as spoken resources with functions, explains how writing would differ, and answers with natural spoken grammar while keeping tense, negation and reference clear.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Recognises the features but labels them as errors, or answers in written-style sentences that are accurate but slow and hard to follow in real time.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Does not notice the features, or makes errors in tense, negation or reference that obscure the answer.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional (UG and PG) learners meet the topic in seminar and group-work preparation, with the emphasis on recognising spoken features in lectures and discussion and on accuracy priorities for assessed speaking. Undergraduate in-sessional work links it to seminars and group projects; PGT learners revisit it when supervision meetings or lab discussions become frequent. In EMI and transnational settings, models should include proficient speakers who use English as an additional language, not only speakers of one variety. Accept multiple modes of participation for learners who stammer, are autistic or have hearing impairments, and judge the grammar of what they contribute rather than its speed.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-21): added as a new topic. 'Heads and tails' is the usual pedagogical label; the Longman grammar (Biber et al., 1999) describes the same features as prefaces and noun-phrase tags. No source in the bibliography tests whether teaching spoken grammar improves seminar performance, so the activities are proposals. Suggested downstream links (for the SEM, PRS and PRG authors): sem.* discussion topics and prs.* delivery topics may take this topic as a soft prerequisite.

guidance.summary: Academic English has three main ways of relating two nouns: the s-genitive, the of-phrase and noun premodification. The Longman grammar describes the choice as influenced by the animacy of the modifying noun, its length and the given–new organisation of the phrase, and shows that the options are distributed differently across registers (Biber et al., 1999); Biber and Gray (2016) document the long-term growth of noun premodifiers in academic writing. Teach the choice as a set of trade-offs rather than rules, address the school rule against inanimate 's directly, and present of-chains as a readability problem rather than a grammar error.

activities.title: Three ways to say it
learnerActions: Collect ten examples of each form from articles in their field
Sort them by whether the modifying noun is a person, an organisation or place, or another inanimate noun, and note the length of each modifier
State two tendencies they observe and test them on three new phrases
activities.intendedInsight: Genitive choice follows tendencies of animacy, length and information flow, and inanimate 's is common in real texts.
activities.rationale: Learner-collected examples let the class test the tendencies described in the Longman grammar (Biber et al., 1999) against texts from their own field.

activities.title: Untangling of-chains
learnerActions: Find sentences in own drafts with two or more consecutive of-phrases
Rewrite each in two ways: with a genitive or premodifier, and with a clause
Ask a partner which version is easiest to read and keeps the meaning
activities.intendedInsight: Of-chains can be repaired in several ways, and the best choice depends on what is given and what the reader needs to process.
activities.rationale: Phrasal compression is a central resource of academic prose but leaves relations between nouns implicit (Biber & Gray, 2016), so comparing compressed and expanded versions is intended to build judgement rather than a single rule.

difficulties.pattern: We were taught that 's is only for people, so I always write 'the aims of the study'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Avoidance of inanimate s-genitives and long of-chains (the results of the analysis of the data of the survey).
difficulties.response: Show inanimate genitives in published articles from the learner's field and present the school rule as a simplification. Do not replace it with the opposite rule: of-phrases remain the better choice for long or new modifiers.

difficulties.pattern: In my first language I use one 'of'-type structure for everything, so I do the same in English.
difficulties.revealedBy: Of-phrases where a compound or genitive is conventional (the department of the economics), or reversed noun + noun order, in writers whose first language relates nouns mainly through a postposed genitive or a single linking particle.
difficulties.response: Contrast the English options with the first-language construction, practise conversion in both directions, and accept of-phrases where they are clearer.

difficulties.pattern: The Smith's model … the study' aims …
difficulties.revealedBy: Articles combined with a proper-noun genitive, and apostrophes misplaced with singular and plural possessors.
difficulties.response: Show that a genitive takes the place of the determiner (Smith's model; the authors' model) and return to apostrophe forms for singular and plural possessors. Do not over-correct by removing genitives altogether.

diagnostic.task: Give the phrase 'the results of the analysis of the data of the survey' and two sentences with inanimate genitives, and ask the learner to rewrite the chain and judge the genitives.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Produces at least two clear alternatives to the chain, explains the choice by length and given–new order, and accepts the inanimate genitives as correct.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Repairs the chain but rejects inanimate genitives as wrong, or replaces the chain with an over-dense noun stack.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Cannot produce alternatives, or produces inaccurate genitive forms.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional UG learners focus on forming genitives accurately and on recognising the three forms in reading. Pre-sessional PG and undergraduate in-sessional learners concentrate on of-chains and field conventions in source-based and report writing. PGT writers revisit the choice when editing dense methods and results sections. Preferences differ somewhat by field and journal, so check models from the learner's target context.
reviewNotes: Review response (R2-11): implemented as a separate topic rather than inside grm.np-premodification, because the choice spans pre- and postmodification. The review's statement that inanimate s-genitives have risen historically in academic prose is not repeated here; the guidance relies on the factors described by Biber et al. (1999) and the growth of noun premodifiers documented by Biber and Gray (2016).

guidance.summary: Intransitive verbs such as occur, happen, arise and emerge have a subject that undergoes rather than performs the event, and second language research describes the passivisation of such verbs (*The problem was happened) as a pattern found across many first-language backgrounds rather than the effect of any single first language (Oshita, 2000). A related group, ergative or change-of-state verbs such as increase, decrease, change, improve and develop, can be used both transitively and intransitively (Biber et al., 1999), so the writer must decide whether to present a change as happening or as caused. Teach both groups together through process description, methods and data commentary, where the voice choice carries meaning.

activities.title: Happened or done?
learnerActions: Sort verbs from a methods section and a results section into three groups: intransitive only (occur, emerge), transitive only (raise, conduct) and both (increase, change)
For each verb in the third group, say whether the writer presents the change as spontaneous or caused, and how the voice shows this
Write three sentences about a process in their field using one verb from each group
activities.intendedInsight: Some verbs have no passive, and for change-of-state verbs voice signals whether an agent caused the change.
activities.rationale: Classifying verbs by transitivity in real texts applies the verb-pattern descriptions in the Longman grammar (Biber et al., 1999) to the learner's field.

activities.title: Trends with and without agents
learnerActions: Describe a line graph twice: once as observed change (unemployment fell) and once as the effect of an intervention (interest rates were raised; costs were reduced)
Compare the two versions and identify which verbs changed voice and which stayed active
Edit own data commentary for forms such as *was occurred and *was increased where no agent is involved
activities.intendedInsight: In data commentary the voice of a change verb shows whether a cause is being claimed.
activities.rationale: Teaching grammars treat the active–passive contrast with ergative verbs as a distinct teaching point (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999); the contrastive task is a proposal rather than a tested intervention.

difficulties.pattern: The problem was happened because… / New issues were emerged.
difficulties.revealedBy: Passive forms of occur, happen, arise, emerge and appear, often in writers who use the passive accurately elsewhere.
difficulties.response: Explain that these verbs describe events with no agent and take no object, so they have no passive; give a short list of academic intransitive verbs and an editing search for was/were + occurred, happened or emerged. Do not treat the error as a sign of weak passive knowledge or reteach the whole passive.

difficulties.pattern: Science writing should be passive, so I write 'the temperature was increased' for every change.
difficulties.revealedBy: Passive change-of-state verbs where no agent is involved (the population was increased over the decade), which imply a cause the writer does not intend.
difficulties.response: Contrast agentless change (the population increased) with caused change (the dose was increased by 10 mg) and ask who, if anyone, made the change happen.

difficulties.pattern: Rise and raise mean the same thing.
difficulties.revealedBy: Transitive verbs used intransitively or the reverse (prices raised sharply; the company rose its prices).
difficulties.response: Teach rise/raise and fall/lower or reduce as intransitive–transitive pairs with their past forms, and practise them in trend descriptions.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to describe a simple before-and-after table in three sentences, one of which must present a change caused by a named intervention.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Uses active intransitive forms for agentless changes, passive or active transitive forms for caused changes, and no passivised intransitive verbs.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Avoids *was occurred but uses passive change verbs where no agent is involved, or confuses rise and raise.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Passivised intransitive verbs, or no consistent link between voice and agency.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners meet these verbs in process description and simple trend description, where accurate forms are the priority. Pre-sessional UG and PG learners apply the agent distinction in data commentary and methods writing. Undergraduate in-sessional work addresses it through lab reports and data-heavy assignments, and PGT writers revisit it in self-editing. The topic matters most in fields that describe processes and trends, such as the sciences, engineering and economics.
reviewNotes: Review response (R2-12): added as a new topic; grm.passive-voice keeps a short mastery statement and cross-reference. Of the three SLA sources named in the review (Zobl, 1989; Yip, 1995; Oshita, 2000), only Oshita (2000) is listed under this file's proposedReferences, because one source is enough for the guidance claim. Suggested downstream links (for the FUN and DAT authors): fun.describing-process and dat.describing-trends may take this topic as a soft prerequisite.

guidance.summary: Sentence-type labels are useful mainly as tools for punctuation and controlled clause combining. Teach them by counting finite clauses, and challenge the common classroom equation of 'complex' with 'better': corpus research shows that academic prose is distinguished by dense noun phrases rather than by many dependent clauses (Biber & Gray, 2010), so a long single-clause sentence can be both 'simple' and difficult. Celce-Murcia and Larsen-Freeman (1999) provide a pedagogical account of coordination and subordination that supports this clause-based approach.

activities.title: Count the finite verbs
learnerActions: Underline every finite verb in eight sentences from a textbook in their field
Use the count and the joining devices to classify each sentence
Find the longest sentence with only one finite verb and discuss why it is long
activities.intendedInsight: Sentence type depends on clauses, not length; long academic sentences are often single clauses with heavy noun phrases.
activities.rationale: Clause counting gives an objective basis for classification and leads directly into the corpus finding that academic complexity is largely phrasal (Biber & Gray, 2010).

activities.title: Combining for a purpose
learnerActions: Take three short related sentences about a topic in their field
Combine them in two ways: once with a coordinator and once with a subordinator
Explain how each version presents the relation between the ideas and which idea becomes the main point
activities.intendedInsight: Coordination presents ideas as equal; subordination ranks them, so the choice affects meaning.
activities.rationale: Focusing on the meaning of clause-combining choices follows a form–meaning–use approach to grammar (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

difficulties.pattern: A long sentence is a complex sentence, and complex sentences are better.
difficulties.revealedBy: Misclassification of long simple sentences, and writing that strings clauses together to appear sophisticated, often encouraged by test preparation.
difficulties.response: Use clause counting and show expert sentences that are long but single-clause. Do not discourage subordination, which is still needed for argument.

difficulties.pattern: I join my ideas with commas inside one long sentence.
difficulties.revealedBy: Several independent clauses linked by commas, in writers whose first-language punctuation allows commas to link clauses within one sentence.
difficulties.response: Show the English convention that independent clauses need a coordinator, semicolon or full stop, and link to the sentence-boundary repair strategies.

diagnostic.task: Give six textbook sentences, including a long single-clause sentence, and ask the learner to mark clause boundaries and classify each.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct classification based on finite clauses, including the long simple sentence, with joining devices identified.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct for short sentences but misclassifies the long simple sentence or misses a relative clause.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Classifies by length or punctuation alone.

guidance.contextNotes: At foundation level the concept is taught explicitly and linked to punctuation and paragraph writing. On pre-sessional courses it is reviewed briefly, with the emphasis shifting to the misconception that complexity means length.

guidance.summary: Fragments are among the 'treatable' rule-governed errors in Ferris's (1999) sense, and comma splices and fused sentences follow similarly clear rules, well suited to explicit teaching and self-editing. Teach four repair strategies and ask learners to choose by meaning, so that boundary editing also improves logical clarity. Separate genuine boundary errors from style prescriptions: Chang and Swales (1999) found that features such as sentence-initial conjunctions, often proscribed in style advice, do occur in expert academic writing, so 'never start with And or But' should not be taught as a rule.

activities.title: Four ways to fix a splice
learnerActions: Take one comma splice and repair it four ways: full stop, semicolon, coordinator, subordination
Discuss how each repair changes the relation between the ideas
Repair five more splices from own drafts, choosing the best option for each
activities.intendedInsight: There is more than one correct repair, and the best one expresses the intended logical relation.
activities.rationale: Ferris (1999) lists sentence fragments among the more 'treatable' error types; extending the same explicit-repair approach to comma splices and fused sentences is an analogy rather than a tested claim.

activities.title: Fragment or style?
learnerActions: Sort ten sentences into boundary errors (fragments, splices) and acceptable style choices (a sentence beginning with 'But', a short emphatic sentence)
Justify each decision
Check own writing for detached because-, which- and such as-fragments
activities.intendedInsight: Boundary rules concern clause structure; many 'rules' about sentence openings are style prescriptions, not grammar.
activities.rationale: Chang and Swales (1999) show that some informal elements proscribed by style advice appear in expert academic prose, so learners need to separate grammar from style lore.

difficulties.pattern: Because the sample was small. This limits the findings.
difficulties.revealedBy: Detached subordinate clauses punctuated as sentences, often reflecting spoken answer patterns.
difficulties.response: Teach the test 'Can this stand alone as a statement?' and attach detached clauses to the adjacent main clause.

difficulties.pattern: The results were significant, however the sample was small.
difficulties.revealedBy: Comma splices with linking adverbials, often alongside correct use of 'but'.
difficulties.response: Contrast conjunctions with linking adverbials and show the semicolon and full-stop repairs.

difficulties.pattern: I was told never to start a sentence with 'And' or 'But'.
difficulties.revealedBy: Awkward avoidance strategies, or learners marking correct sentences as errors in peer review.
difficulties.response: Present the practice as a style choice that varies by field and formality, and focus attention on genuine boundary errors.

diagnostic.task: Give a 120-word paragraph with two comma splices, one fragment and one fused sentence, and ask the learner to find and repair them using at least three strategies.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All four errors found and repaired, with repairs that express the logical relations.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most errors found, but repairs default to full stops or one error type is missed.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Few errors found, or correct sentences altered.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional UG learners need explicit teaching and repeated editing practice, and boundary errors are assessed directly in their writing. Pre-sessional PG learners usually need a short review and an editing routine rather than full teaching. In undergraduate in-sessional work, the focus is on a quick editing pass for splices and fragments in assessed drafts.
reviewNotes: Chang and Swales (1999) include sentence-initial conjunctions among the ten informal features they examined.

guidance.summary: Teach commas as markers of grammatical structure: most academic comma decisions follow from recognising introductory elements, non-defining clauses, appositives and list items, and from avoiding commas that separate a subject from its verb or a verb from its object. Present genuinely variable conventions, such as the serial comma (required in APA style and recommended by Chicago, but optional in many British house styles), as choices to apply consistently (American Psychological Association, 2020; University of Chicago Press, 2024).

activities.title: Restore and justify
learnerActions: Restore commas in a paragraph from which they have been removed
Justify each comma with a structural reason (introductory clause, non-defining clause, list, appositive)
Compare with the original and discuss any differences that are matters of style
activities.intendedInsight: Most commas can be justified by structure, and some are optional.
activities.rationale: Linking punctuation to structure makes it learnable and transferable; style guides document which uses are optional (American Psychological Association, 2020).

activities.title: Commas that change meaning
learnerActions: Compare sentence pairs that differ only in commas (non-defining versus defining clauses; lists with and without the serial comma)
Explain the meaning difference in each pair
Find a sentence in own writing where a comma decision affects meaning and revise it
activities.intendedInsight: Some commas are semantic, not decorative.
activities.rationale: Meaning-focused contrasts make punctuation decisions principled (Celce-Murcia & Larsen-Freeman, 1999).

difficulties.pattern: I put a comma where I would pause when speaking.
difficulties.revealedBy: Commas between long subjects and their verbs, or before that-clauses.
difficulties.response: Replace the pause rule with structural rules and practise with long-subject sentences.

difficulties.pattern: Which always needs a comma.
difficulties.revealedBy: Commas around defining which-clauses.
difficulties.response: Return to the meaning distinction between defining and non-defining clauses.

difficulties.pattern: Commas are not important; the marker will understand.
difficulties.revealedBy: Little attention to commas in editing despite feedback.
difficulties.response: Show examples where comma choices change meaning or cause misreading, and include commas in a short editing pass.

diagnostic.task: Give a 100-word paragraph without commas and ask the learner to restore them and justify three.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Commas placed correctly with structural justifications, no subject–verb commas, and a consistent serial-comma choice.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Most commas correct but one subject–verb comma or a missed non-defining clause.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Commas placed by pause or at random.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners focus on introductory elements, lists and relative clauses, and commas are assessed directly. Pre-sessional learners focus on non-defining clauses, appositives and consistency with a department's style guide. In-sessional UG and PGT learners revisit commas through self-access and proofreading checklists.

guidance.summary: Semicolons and colons are useful in dense academic prose because they signal relations inside the sentence: the semicolon balances related independent clauses or separates complex list items, while the colon introduces an expansion of what precedes it. Teach the complete-clause test for colons and the comparable-weight test for semicolons, and present style variation (for example capitalisation after a colon, which differs between APA and Chicago) as a matter of consistency (American Psychological Association, 2020; University of Chicago Press, 2024).

activities.title: Balance or expand?
learnerActions: Sort sentence pairs into those whose relation is balance (semicolon) and those whose second part explains or lists (colon)
Punctuate each accordingly
Write one sentence of each type about their own topic
activities.intendedInsight: Semicolons balance; colons expand.
activities.rationale: A functional contrast makes the choice between the marks principled; style guides describe both functions (University of Chicago Press, 2024).

activities.title: Complex lists
learnerActions: Look at a list whose items contain commas (for example study locations with cities and countries)
Repunctuate it with semicolons
Check a list in own writing for the same issue
activities.intendedInsight: Semicolons prevent confusion in lists whose items contain commas.
activities.rationale: Style manuals specify this use for clarity in seriation (American Psychological Association, 2020).

difficulties.pattern: The factors include: cost, access and quality.
difficulties.revealedBy: Colons after verbs or prepositions that already introduce the list.
difficulties.response: Teach the complete-clause test and show two repairs (delete the colon; add 'the following').

difficulties.pattern: Semicolons look academic, so I use them often.
difficulties.revealedBy: Semicolons between a clause and a phrase, or in most sentences of a paragraph.
difficulties.response: Restrict semicolons to joining complete, closely related clauses and to complex lists; show how overuse slows reading.

diagnostic.task: Give six sentences needing semicolon or colon decisions and ask the learner to correct and justify them.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Correct choices justified by the complete-clause and balance tests.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Correct semicolons but colon errors after verbs, or vice versa.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Marks used interchangeably or at random.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation learners meet colons for lists and semicolons as a splice repair. Pre-sessional and in-sessional learners use both in dense explanatory and argumentative writing and apply the target style consistently.

guidance.summary: These conventions are small, but markers and editors notice them first, and some carry meaning. Hyphens disambiguate compound modifiers, apostrophes signal possession, and ellipsis and square brackets let writers fit a quotation into their own sentence provided the source's meaning is preserved, which is part of faithful source use as well as formatting (Pecorari, 2013). Other conventions vary by style: APA and Chicago use double quotation marks and place commas and full stops inside closing marks, many British house styles use single marks and place punctuation by sense, and APA uses sentence case for article titles in the reference list where MLA uses title case (American Psychological Association, 2020; Modern Language Association of America, 2021; University of Chicago Press, 2024). Teach the meaning-bearing conventions as principles, teach the style required in the learner's context thoroughly, and build a final mechanics pass into editing.

activities.title: Integrate without distorting
learnerActions: Quote part of a 60-word source passage in their own sentence
Use an ellipsis to omit a phrase and square brackets to change one word to fit their grammar, with a citation in the required style
Ask a partner to compare the quotation with the original and confirm that the meaning has not changed
activities.intendedInsight: Ellipsis and brackets are tools for integration that must preserve the source's meaning.
activities.rationale: Accurate representation of sources is central to good source use (Pecorari, 2013), and style guides specify how changes to a quotation are marked (American Psychological Association, 2020).

activities.title: Hyphen, apostrophe or capital?
learnerActions: Sort phrases into compound modifiers before a noun, the same words after a noun, and -ly adverb + adjective combinations, and hyphenate only the first group
Sort terms from their field into proper nouns, named theories and general concepts, checking uncertain cases in a recent journal in their field
Audit every apostrophe and capital on one page of own writing and correct plural-acronym and decade apostrophes (PhD's, 1990's)
activities.intendedInsight: Hyphens depend on position before the noun, apostrophes mark possession rather than plurals, and capitals mark names rather than importance.
activities.rationale: Linking each convention to a structural principle is intended to make it more transferable than a memorised list; style manuals describe the same principles (American Psychological Association, 2020; University of Chicago Press, 2024).

activities.title: Same text, two styles
learnerActions: Format the same quotation and the same two references in the style required by their course and in one other style
List the differences in quotation marks, punctuation placement and capitalisation of titles
Check a draft and its reference list against the required style
activities.intendedInsight: Quotation-mark and capitalisation conventions are style choices; consistency with the required style is what is assessed.
activities.rationale: Comparing style manuals makes the variation explicit (Modern Language Association of America, 2021; University of Chicago Press, 2024).

difficulties.pattern: I removed some words so the quotation supports my point better.
difficulties.revealedBy: Ellipses that remove qualifications or negations from the source.
difficulties.response: Discuss fidelity to meaning as an integrity issue and have learners check each quotation against the original.

difficulties.pattern: The participant's responses (meaning several participants) … the PhD's … a well known model.
difficulties.revealedBy: Singular possessives for plural owners, apostrophes in plurals, and missing or misplaced hyphens in compound modifiers.
difficulties.response: Teach the owner-first check (write the owner noun, then add 's or ') and the before-the-noun test for hyphens. If the learner cannot find the head noun, return to noun-phrase premodification.

difficulties.pattern: Important ideas should have capitals, like Globalisation and Sustainability.
difficulties.revealedBy: Capitals on general concepts used for emphasis, and inconsistent capitalisation of the same key term.
difficulties.response: Explain that capitals signal names, not importance, and show examples from journals in the learner's field.

difficulties.pattern: The full stop always goes inside the quotation marks. / My reference manager decides the capitals.
difficulties.revealedBy: Citation and full-stop placement that follows one style's rule in another style, and reference lists in mixed title and sentence case imported from different databases.
difficulties.response: Teach the target style's placement for run-in and block quotations with models, and add a final consistency check of quotations and reference-list capitalisation.

diagnostic.task: Ask the learner to quote part of a short passage in their own sentence, omitting a phrase and changing one word, with a citation in the specified style, and to correct a five-line extract containing apostrophe, hyphen, dash and capitalisation errors.
diagnostic.strongResponse: A faithful quotation with correct ellipsis, brackets and citation placement, and all mechanics corrected consistently with the named style, with the principles (owner first, before the noun, names not importance) explained.
diagnostic.partialResponse: A faithful quotation with one formatting error, or mechanics corrected in some categories but not applied consistently.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Unmarked changes to the quotation, or several errors in each category.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional UG learners are taught apostrophes, compound modifiers, capitals and basic quotation punctuation explicitly, because these are checked in their assessed writing. Pre-sessional PG learners extend this to ellipsis, brackets and block quotations in literature-based projects, largely through checklists and feedback. In-sessional UG and PGT learners revisit the conventions through self-access guides and proofreading checklists matched to their department's referencing style rather than taught sessions. Conventions differ between US styles, British house styles and journals elsewhere, so the target is the style required in the learner's context. Learners with dyslexia or visual impairments may find a separate mechanics pass with text-to-speech or a style checker helpful, and markers should avoid treating mechanics as evidence of understanding.
reviewNotes: Review response (R1-19): sen.capitalisation and sen.quotation-punctuation are merged into this topic; their mastery evidence, assessment and difficulties are carried over in condensed form. Number and unit style moved to num.number-expressions.

Review response (R1-07): the topic is not core beyond pre-sessional UG. For in-sessional UG and PGT it is marked 'revisit' (self-access and proofreading guidance) rather than removed, because dissertations still require quotation and reference-list conventions.

guidance.summary: Sentence length is a weak index of academic quality. Lu (2011) found that some length-based measures discriminated proficiency levels, but length is a by-product of other choices, and Biber and Gray (2010) show that academic complexity lies mainly in noun phrases rather than in long chains of clauses. Halliday's (1989) contrast between the grammatical intricacy of speech and the lexical density of writing helps explain why clause-heavy long sentences read like transcribed speech. Teach length as a readability choice: split overloaded sentences, combine short ones when relations need stating, and use short sentences for emphasis.

activities.title: Split, combine, emphasise
learnerActions: Take a paragraph from own writing and mark the longest and shortest sentences
Split any sentence that contains more than one main claim, and combine any run of short sentences whose relation is unstated
Add or keep one short sentence to state the paragraph's key point and read the result aloud to a partner
activities.intendedInsight: Length should follow purpose: explanation can be long, key claims can be short.
activities.rationale: Treating length as an outcome of information management rather than a target follows the corpus finding that academic complexity is mainly phrasal (Biber & Gray, 2010).

activities.title: Intricate versus dense
learnerActions: Compare a long, clause-heavy student sentence with a long, noun-phrase-heavy published sentence
Count clauses and noun-phrase modifiers in each
Rewrite the student sentence to reduce clauses while keeping its content
activities.intendedInsight: Long sentences in speech-like writing are intricate; long sentences in academic writing are dense; expert readers often process dense sentences in their field efficiently, but density also leaves relations implicit, so neither kind is automatically easier.
activities.rationale: Halliday's (1989) distinction between grammatical intricacy and lexical density explains the difference and offers a revision target.

difficulties.pattern: Longer sentences get higher marks.
difficulties.revealedBy: Very long sentences joined with and, which and so, often trained in test preparation.
difficulties.response: Show reader-processing problems with examples and expert paragraphs with varied length. Do not set arbitrary maximum word counts.

difficulties.pattern: I write short sentences so I do not make mistakes.
difficulties.revealedBy: Strings of short simple sentences with no explicit relations, typically from learners anxious about accuracy.
difficulties.response: Encourage combining with secure structures (non-finite clauses, phrasal coordination) and frame occasional errors as part of development.

diagnostic.task: Give a 150-word paragraph with one 70-word sentence and a run of five very short sentences, and ask the learner to revise it for readability and explain two decisions.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Long sentence split at logical points, short sentences combined with explicit relations, key claim prominent, and decisions explained by reader processing.
diagnostic.partialResponse: One of the two problems addressed, or both addressed without explicit relations.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Little change or new boundary errors.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional learners revise habits formed in test preparation. Undergraduate and PGT in-sessional learners apply length control to extended assessed writing, often in response to feedback on readability.
reviewNotes: Lu (2011) reports group-level discrimination of proficiency by several measures; it is not cited as evidence that longer sentences are better.

guidance.summary: Concision is the removal of words that add nothing, not the removal of everything optional. Snow and Uccelli (2009) list concision among the features that characterise academic language, but Hyland's (2005) work on metadiscourse shows that hedges, signposts and engagement markers do real interpersonal and organisational work, so they should not be cut as padding. Biber and Gray (2016) show that compression is a long-term trend in academic writing; concision teaching should therefore target empty wordiness while preserving purposeful compression and necessary qualification.

activities.title: Cut by 20 per cent
learnerActions: Take a 300-word passage from own writing and cut it by 20 per cent
Label each cut as wordy phrase, redundant pair, empty light-verb construction or unnecessary repetition
Ask a partner to check that no content, hedges or necessary signposts were lost
activities.intendedInsight: Most drafts contain removable words, but some apparently optional words carry meaning.
activities.rationale: Concision is a feature of academic language (Snow & Uccelli, 2009); peer checking guards against cutting metadiscourse that does real work (Hyland, 2005).

activities.title: Padding or purpose?
learnerActions: Sort phrases from a paragraph into padding (due to the fact that, it is important to note that) and purposeful metadiscourse (this suggests that, in contrast)
Rewrite the paragraph, removing only the padding
Compare the effect on readability
activities.intendedInsight: Metadiscourse is not padding; only empty phrases should go.
activities.rationale: Hyland's (2005) model shows that metadiscourse organises text and engages readers.

difficulties.pattern: More words show more knowledge, and I need to reach the word count.
difficulties.revealedBy: Padding to reach minimum word counts, often from assessment contexts that rewarded length.
difficulties.response: Explain that many university assignments set maximum rather than minimum limits and reward density of argument, although practice varies between institutions and countries; check the local rule in the learner's target context and practise cutting.

difficulties.pattern: I cut all the hedges and linking words to save space.
difficulties.revealedBy: Over-cut texts that make unqualified claims and lack signposting.
difficulties.response: Restore hedges and signposts and teach the padding-versus-purpose distinction.

difficulties.pattern: We carried out an investigation into the analysis of the data.
difficulties.revealedBy: Light verbs with stacked nominalisations.
difficulties.response: Replace with the verb (we analysed the data) and keep nominalisations that summarise or link.

diagnostic.task: Give a 200-word padded paragraph with one necessary hedge and ask the learner to cut it by about 20 per cent.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Padding removed, hedge and key signposts kept, meaning unchanged and no new errors.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Padding reduced but the hedge removed, or cuts made with one meaning change.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Little reduction or substantial loss of meaning.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional UG learners meet concision mainly as removing padding. Pre-sessional PG learners are taught it explicitly for word-limited extended projects. PGT in-sessional learners apply it in dissertations and reports, where word limits are a constant pressure, and undergraduate in-sessional learners in assessed reports. PGR writers focus on article word limits and abstract writing.
reviewNotes: Snow and Uccelli (2009) are cited for concision as one of the features that characterise academic language, not for any claim about how concision should be taught.
Review response (R6-11): the IELTS Lexical Resource link was removed, because concision is taught here for word-limited academic writing rather than for test preparation.

guidance.summary: The principle of end-weight, described in the Longman grammar (Biber et al., 1999), and the given-before-new tendency of information structure (Halliday & Matthiessen, 2014; Thompson, 2014) together explain why sentences with long subjects and late verbs are hard to read. Because academic writing packs meaning into heavy noun phrases, often leaving relations implicit (Biber & Gray, 2010), learners need explicit techniques for moving weight to the end: extraposition, the passive, postmodification and splitting. Present these as reader-centred revision choices rather than as rules.

activities.title: Find the verb
learnerActions: Underline the main verb in each sentence of a paragraph of own writing and count the words before it
Revise sentences where the verb comes very late by moving heavy material after the verb or into a separate sentence
Read both versions aloud to a partner and compare ease of understanding
activities.intendedInsight: Readers process sentences more easily when the main verb comes early.
activities.rationale: End-weight is a well-documented tendency of English (Biber et al., 1999), and the counting step makes it visible in learners' own writing.

activities.title: Given first, new last
learnerActions: Mark given and new information in a short published paragraph
Revise a sentence from own writing so that it begins with given information and ends with new or heavy information
Discuss which technique (passive, extraposition, reordering) was used
activities.intendedInsight: End-weight and information flow work together.
activities.rationale: Functional grammar links theme and information structure to clause ordering (Thompson, 2014).

difficulties.pattern: The long subject makes the sentence academic.
difficulties.revealedBy: Sentences with 25+ word subjects before the verb.
difficulties.response: Show revisions that move weight to the end and compare readability.

difficulties.pattern: Long pre-verbal subjects delay the main verb, a pattern common across first-language backgrounds as writers begin to compress information into noun phrases; writers whose first language places modifiers, including relative clauses, before the noun may favour heavy pre-head modification.
difficulties.revealedBy: Heavy pre-verbal material and verbs delayed until the end of long sentences.
difficulties.response: Teach end-weight explicitly and practise moving material after the verb.

diagnostic.task: Give three sentences (a 30-word subject, a five-noun stack, a that-clause subject) and ask the learner to revise each and explain.
diagnostic.strongResponse: All three revised with earlier verbs and later heavy material, explained in terms of processing and information flow.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Two revised effectively, or revisions effective but explained only as preference.
diagnostic.gapResponse: Little change or meaning altered.

guidance.contextNotes: Pre-sessional PG learners at higher entry levels meet end-weight when revising dense literature-based writing. Undergraduate in-sessional learners focus on long subjects in assessed writing. PGT writers apply end-weight in dense methods, results and theoretical writing; for PGR writers it is a core part of revising theses and articles for readability, often in response to supervisor or reviewer feedback.

guidance.summary: Lists are a genre-dependent resource: they are conventional in reports, proposals, methods sections, slides and posters but are usually discouraged in essays, where connected prose is expected to make relations between points explicit. Style manuals give rules for run-in and vertical lists, including parallel construction and punctuation (American Psychological Association, 2020; University of Chicago Press, 2024). Teach list formatting together with the skill of converting lists into connected paragraphs.

activities.title: Fix the list
learnerActions: Correct a bullet list with a fragmentary lead-in, non-parallel items and inconsistent punctuation
Explain each correction
Check a list in own writing against the same criteria
activities.intendedInsight: Good lists have a grammatical lead-in, parallel items and consistent punctuation.
activities.rationale: Style manuals describe these requirements (American Psychological Association, 2020).

activities.title: From bullets to prose
learnerActions: Take a bullet list from a report or slide
Rewrite it as a paragraph that states the relations between the items
Compare which version would suit an essay and which a report
activities.intendedInsight: Converting lists into prose requires making relations explicit, which is what essays demand.
activities.rationale: Moving between list and prose forms develops awareness of genre conventions and of the linking work that a list leaves undone; this is a practitioner proposal rather than a tested procedure.

difficulties.pattern: Bullet points are clearer, so I use them in essays.
difficulties.revealedBy: Bullet lists in essays, often from professional or slide-based writing experience.
difficulties.response: Explain genre expectations and practise conversion to prose.

difficulties.pattern: My list items are all different forms.
difficulties.revealedBy: Non-parallel list items.
difficulties.response: Add a parallelism check to editing.

diagnostic.task: Give a flawed bullet list and ask the learner to fix it and rewrite it as an essay paragraph.
diagnostic.strongResponse: Corrected list with parallel items and consistent punctuation, and a paragraph that adds explicit links.
diagnostic.partialResponse: Corrected list but a paragraph that strings items together without links.
diagnostic.gapResponse: List errors persist and no conversion.

guidance.contextNotes: Foundation and pre-sessional learners focus on list formatting and genre awareness. Undergraduate in-sessional learners apply list conventions in reports and proposals. PGT learners revisit them through self-access and proofreading checklists rather than taught sessions.
reviewNotes: The claim that essays usually discourage bullet lists reflects practitioner consensus and departmental guidance rather than a cited study; local briefs should be checked.
Review response (R1-07): rather than removing the PGT stage, the topic is marked 'revisit' there, meaning self-access and proofreading guidance, so it does not enter the core PGT pathway.

authorNotes: Overlap: grm.error-monitoring and edt.grammar-editing both cover targeted checking of recurrent errors. Suggest scoping grm.error-monitoring as the strategic, longitudinal routine (logging and prioritising personal error patterns) and edt.grammar-editing as the in-draft editing procedure, with edt.grammar-editing taking grm.error-monitoring as a prerequisite.

Overlap: grm.passive-voice and grm.non-finite-clauses both list dangling modifiers in their skeleton scope. I treat dangling participles mainly in grm.non-finite-clauses and mention them in grm.passive-voice only where a passive main clause creates the dangle; consider removing them from the passive scope note.

Overlap: grm.relative-clauses and sen.commas both cover punctuation of non-defining clauses; grm.linking-adverbial-placement overlaps sen.semicolons-colons and coh.linking-adverbials. Consider moving grm.linking-adverbial-placement to SEN, where punctuation topics sit.

Overlap: grm.reporting-structures with src.reporting-verbs (which absorbed src.signal-phrases after review R1-37). I scoped grm.reporting-structures to complementation patterns and did not link to SRC topics to avoid cycles; R1-37 suggests src.reporting-verbs take grm.reporting-structures as a hard prerequisite.
Cross-strand cycle risk: grm.tense-in-reporting takes src.citation-forms as a soft prerequisite. If the SRC author makes src.citation-forms depend on grm.tense-in-reporting, drop my edge.
Overlap: grm.reference-pronouns ('this + summarising noun') with coh.signalling-nouns and voc.abstract-shell-nouns. Suggest coh.signalling-nouns take grm.reference-pronouns as a prerequisite.

Overlap: grm.phrasal-complexity with reg.spoken-vs-written and reg.information-density. I used reg.register-awareness as the prerequisite to avoid a likely cycle; editors should decide one direction between grm.phrasal-complexity and reg.spoken-vs-written.

Overlap: sen.concision and sen.clarity-end-weight with edt.style-editing and reg.information-density; suggest edt.style-editing take both as prerequisites. sen.punctuation-mechanics (which absorbed capitalisation and quotation punctuation) and sen.lists-bullets touch wpr.formatting, ess.headings and cit.reference-list.

Possible merge: grm.fronting-inversion and grm.clefts-emphasis could be one 'focus and marked word order' topic; fronting and inversion are infrequent in academic prose and are mainly a reading and PGR refinement point.

Gaps: no topic covers scope of negation and quantifiers (All X are not…; not … any; only placement), verb complementation with -ing versus to-infinitive (aim to, avoid doing, contribute to doing), or noun-phrase apposition as a definitional resource beyond the brief mention in grm.np-postmodification. Mandative subjunctive is placed under fun.recommending, which seems right.

Entry points: grm.clause-elements and grm.tense-aspect are the intended entry points in GRM/SEN; the soft edge grm.tense-aspect <- grm.clause-elements was removed after review R1-25 because tense is taught from the start of any programme and the edge made clause analysis a spurious gate.

Revision (post-review): new topics grm.spoken-grammar, grm.genitive-noun-modifiers and grm.unaccusative-verbs. Suggested incoming edges for other groups: sem.* and prs.* delivery topics <- grm.spoken-grammar (soft); fun.describing-process and dat.describing-trends <- grm.unaccusative-verbs (soft). reg.spoken-vs-written and grm.spoken-grammar are deliberately unlinked to avoid a cross-file cycle; editors should choose one direction.
